textes.Mon plus beau déguisement ? Une moustach: My best disguise? A moustache, a beret and an accent. I played pétanque in Port-Azur for a whole afternoon, with a certain Raymond. I lost the jack. Well… a jack was lost. It might not have been me.
textes.Mon plus beau graffiti, c'est sur le Mur: My best graffiti is on the Expression Wall, to the west: two hands helping each other. All of Boucan put their handprints around it. Even Chaussette's dogs. There's a footprint from Boulon. He slipped.
textes.Mon plus beau poème n'a pas de rime du t: My most beautiful poem has no rhyme at all. I wrote it the day we understood we would never go back to Ondelune. It's one line long: “Here too, there are stars.” I've never read it to anyone. Except you.
textes.Mon plus grand chantier, c'est le châtea: My biggest job is the water tower. Twenty-eight metres. Bardane held me on a rope, Lentille sent our soup up on a pulley. Three weeks. At the top, a rat playing guitar; in the middle, seagulls; at the bottom, the names of all the inhabitants. When we finished, the whole town applauded from below.
textes.Mon plus grand exploit ? (Il bombe le to: My greatest feat? (He puffs out his chest, then deflates it.) Friend… I'll confess something. They're all lost in the fog. All of them. I need a REAL feat. With a witness. And sunshine. Deep in the Goblin Wood, the goblins have a camp, and a chief, and a banner decorated with the feathers from the guards' helmets. Defeat him with me, or in front of me, or even a little in my place, and bring back the banner. I, SIR TANCRÈDE DE TOURNEVENT, swear to follow you afterwards to the ends of the earth!
textes.Mon plus grand échec : une cape anti-fou: My greatest failure: an anti-lightning cape for Violette. Silk lining, silver thread, three weeks of work. It caught fire at the first bolt. Violette said “… it happens”. I cried. Then we laughed, the two of us, in the middle of the smoke. Since then we've been trying together. We're on cape number nine.
My longest sermon lasted five hours. Well, it lasted ten minutes, then I fell asleep for four hours and fifty minutes. The faithful stayed. They slept too. When I woke up, everyone was rested and happy. The Baron said it was the best sermon of his life. He was wearing a pillow-shaped hat.
textes.Mon pointeur ! Tu fais équipe avec moi,: My pointer! You're on my team next time. Marcel's already shaking.
textes.Mon poisson, comment t'oublier ? Ta prem: My little fish, how could I forget you? Your first spoonful of samphire soup: eyes wide, then shut tight. Like everyone. But you smiled.
textes.Mon pote ! Tu tombes bien, Mistral va lâ: My mate! Perfect timing, Mistral's about to drop a big one.
textes.Mon premier arbre, je l'ai planté à six: I planted my first tree when I was six. An apple pip, in a flowerpot. I talked to it every evening. My parents laughed. At ten, it was taller than me. At twenty, it was giving apples. It's still there, at the end of the second terrace. We say hello to each other.
textes.Mon premier bijou, je l'ai fait avec un: My first jewel, I made it from a bolt that fell off a wagon and a sliver of crystal. I gave it to my grandmother. She wore it round her neck to the very end. She used to say: “It's not the gold that makes a jewel. It's the hand that made it.”
textes.Mon premier bonjour, je l'ai dit à un pi: I said my first hello to a pigeon. It had flown into the lobby by mistake. It did not answer. I noted: “pigeon, rude”. Since then, I have amended my note: “pigeon, shy”.
textes.Mon premier boulon, je l'ai trouvé à tro: I found my first bolt when I was three, under Mum's anvil. I put it in my mouth. Mum shouted so loud the forge stopped. Since then, I don't put bolts in my mouth. I put them in boxes. It's less fun, but it's cleaner.
textes.Mon premier cerf-volant, c'est Grand-Pèr: My first kite was made by Grandpa Séverin, out of an old tablecloth and two sticks. It was all lopsided. It flew anyway, really high. The wind carried it over the edge. I watched it go down towards the sea. I cried, then I thought it was beautiful: at least it got to go down there.
textes.Mon premier client était un robot aspira: My first customer was a robot vacuum. It wanted a program to vacuum faster. I sold it “Turbo-Vac”. It vacuums very fast now. It vacuums socks too. And cats. Well, it tries. The cats won't have it.
textes.Mon premier client, c'était la boulanger: My first customer was Honorine's bakery. I carried the sack myself, fifty kilos, from the mill up to the Middle Town. Outside her door, I heard her singing. I stood there, sack on my shoulder, until the end of the song. She opened the door. I said: “I'm catching my breath.” I've been catching my breath for ten years.
textes.Mon premier coucher de soleil, je l'ai p: I painted my first sunset on the Glass Belvedere, lying on the floor with my head over the void. The sun passed beneath the island and lit the clouds from underneath. I thought the world was gently burning. I cried onto the canvas. It has little spots. I kept them.
textes.Mon premier dessin, je l'ai fait avec un: My first drawing, I did with a lump of coal that fell from a boiler. A black line on a container door. It looked like a cat. The Fronde's real cat walked past, looked at it, and sat down next to it. Since then, I believe drawings can call things to them.
textes.Mon premier dessin, je l'ai fait à trois: I did my first drawing when I was three, on the wall of the bike workshop, with engine grease. It was Tornade falling over. Mum didn't wipe it off. It's still there, above the workbench. She says it's my early work. I'd already figured out the main subject of my career.
textes.Mon premier examen, à dix ans : le gâtea: My first exam, at ten: the mooncake hidden by Mère-Lune. I followed the trail all morning. Under the stump, there was half the cake left, and tanuki tracks all around, wide, happy ones. Bedaine told me later he was “checking the hiding place”. With his teeth, apparently.
textes.Mon premier fanzine, je l'ai fait à douz: I made my first fanzine at twelve, on the school photocopier. It was a letter to a girl in my class. I pressed “300” instead of “1”. The whole school read it. So did she. She corrected my mistakes in red pen and gave it back to me. We're still friends.
textes.Mon premier groupe s'appelait Les Boulon: My first band was called the Howling Bolts. There were four of us, with three instruments. The fourth one howled: that was me. Then they gave me a drum kit, so I'd stop howling. I howled while drumming. And that's how I found my style.

My first band was called the Screaming Bolts. There were four of us, and we had three instruments. The fourth one screamed. That was me. Then they gave me a drum kit so I'd stop. I didn't stop. I just screamed while I hit things.
textes.Mon premier jour de serveur : douze tass: My first day as a waiter: twelve cups, one by one, on the tiled floor, right in front of the owner. At the thirteenth, a little girl planted herself in front of me: “You hold the tray with your hand open. Not like a fish.” It was Gisèle, aged ten. She was right. I never broke another thing. Almost.
textes.Mon premier jour de travail, une mouette: On my first day at work, a seagull landed on my head. I was afraid of making it fall. I stayed perfectly still for three days. The quay came to a halt. The containers waited. Then it flew off. Ever since, I do everything very gently.
textes.Mon premier jour de vigie tout seul, j'a: My first day on watch alone, I saw a white shape zip between the trees, faster than the wind. I shouted “Alert! Alert!” with all my might. My uncle came back up, grumbling, eighty steps. It was Bondi training. He said: “A fast rabbit is not an alert.” For a runner it is!
textes.Mon premier jour, j'ai fait une lumière: On my first day, I made a black light. The whole courtyard turned to night, at noon. Aurélien clapped, the others screamed, and the archmage took out a pencil to write down my formula. I've never managed to do it again since. Nobody has. She says it's a unique spell. I say it's a lost spell.
textes.Mon premier matin ici, Mistral a passé l: My first morning here, Mistral played the really soft track, the sunrise one. I sat down in the sand and cried like a little kid. He looked at me from behind his decks and let the track play through twice. He never does that. He said afterwards it was an accident.
textes.Mon premier nuage s'appelait Bernard. J': My first cloud was called Bernard. I was four. It was shaped like a sleeping dog. It lasted six minutes. I cried. My mother told me: “There'll be others.” She was right. I've named forty-two thousand. Bernard is on the first page of my notebook. He always will be.
textes.Mon premier patch des Rats de Cale, Velo: My first Bilge Rats patch — Velours sewed it onto my leather jacket while I was asleep on the bench in the square. When I woke up, there it was. I said “Mh”. She understood it was a huge thank-you.
textes.Mon premier pont à moi, c'est celui de l: My very own first bridge is the west one. I hung singing-stones underneath. On opening day, the wind got up, the bridge danced, sang… and Bedaine got seasick! Later, the Zéphyr's engineers wanted metal bridges. I asked if metal knows how to dance. They went off to take notes somewhere else. Yoo-hoo, bye-bye!
textes.Mon premier pont, je l'ai fait tout seul: My first bridge, I built it all by myself when I was five: two twigs over a puddle, with a hazelnut in the middle for weight. Pomme-de-Pin looked at it very seriously. She blew on it. It danced! She said it was a real bridge. I ate the hazelnut. The bridge sort of collapsed. I kept it anyway.
textes.Mon premier portrait de lui, je l'ai fai: My first portrait of him, I did during a chorus: mouth wide open, eyebrows up. He looked at the drawing and said: “I look like I've got toothache.” It's true, a little. Since then, he plays in profile, facing the sea. He thinks it's punishing me. His profile is magnificent.
textes.Mon premier ruban de Bourgmestre, c'étai: My first ribbon as Burgomaster was for the new wash-house in the Lower Town. I forgot the scissors. Mathilde cut the ribbon with her hammer. It made a tremendous noise and a hole in the cobbles. Since then, I always carry three pairs of scissors. And I no longer ask Mathilde for help.
textes.Mon premier serpent de mer, je l'ai vu à: My first sea serpent, I saw it stone-cold sober. I swear it on my boat. Twenty years ago, on a dead-calm evening, a long dark thing made three humps beside me, then dived. I told the story at the Cauldron. Everyone laughed. So I had a mead, to get over it. Since then, I see them every evening. Nobody believes me any more. It's restful.
textes.Mon premier soir au Perroquet, avec mon: My first evening at the Perroquet, with my first tray, I spilled a whole punch over a big docker. On his shirt, down his neck, everywhere. He didn't even get up. He just said: “It's nothing, it smells nice.” His name was Lucas. I've never got over it. Him, I think he washed his shirt.
textes.Mon premier soir sur la scène de la Guil: My first night on the Guild stage, I sang “Barbe-de-Fer's Dragon”. At the third verse, Master Hugues stood up and wept into his beard. The whole room wept with him. Mamie Rissole handed out handkerchiefs with the pie. Since then he cries at the third verse of every song. It's become my metronome.
textes.Mon premier soir à Port-Coutelas, un pir: My first night in Port-Coutelas, a pirate said I had a face like a log. I answered him politely. With my fist. He slept under the table till morning, and when he woke up, he bought me a grog. That's when I understood Balafre: you hit each other, you get up, you drink together. After that, you're friends. Or you start again.
textes.Mon premier soir, j'ai fait un grand ges: My first night, I made a big gesture and Bastien ended up sitting in the sea, his cap drifting out to sea. I apologised ten times, laughing. He kept saying “It's nothing, it's nothing”, with water up to his waist. He didn't move for a long while. I think he was stunned.
textes.Mon premier soir, j'ai marché dans la me: My first night, I walked into the sea and my feet lit up blue. I screamed. Mistral came down from his decks to explain: “It's plankton.” I said: “Yes, and it's dancing.” He laughed and said: “Exactly.” Since then, plankton officially dances. Mistral said so.
textes.Mon premier soufflet, je l'avais cousu m: My first bellows I sewed myself: it wheezed like a seal with a cold. Today's was made by Nolwenn from an old sail, at fifteen, her first job all on her own. The stitches are a bit crooked. She's offered a hundred times to redo it. I refuse. It blows very well, crooked.
textes.Mon premier vol ! Je ne regarde pas en b: My first flight! I'm not looking down. I'm looking ahead. Ahead is very nice too.
textes.Mon premier vol, je l'ai fait à douze an: I made my first flight at twelve, from the edge of the Falls, with a bedsheet and two brooms. I glided ten metres. Then I fell into the pond. The ducks looked at me like a very big duck. That day, I knew I'd never walk again when I could glide.
textes.Mon premier vrai voyageur, c'était un in: My first real traveller was an engineer from Cliquetis, off the Zéphyr. He fell out of his hammock three times in the night. In the morning, he'd written in chalk on the bulkhead: “Charming. But is a bed too much to ask?” I kept the chalk. That was the day I knew: one day, I'll have beds. Real ones. With legs.
textes.Mon premier étal, c'était une caisse et: My first stall was a crate and a parasol. I was ten. I sold three apples and learned five secrets. That day I understood that people don't just buy fruit. They buy five minutes with someone who listens to them.
textes.Mon prochain canon tirera des pétales de: My next cannon will fire flower petals. The northern shepherds have promised me heather.
textes.Mon professeur de dessin disait que je p: My art teacher said I painted all wrong. Green sky, orange sea. He wrote to my parents. Here, nobody says a thing: the volcano is red, the waterfall is red, the sea is red in places. Next to that, my colours are almost reasonable.
textes.Mon programme : des lanternes sur le qua: My manifesto: lanterns on the quay, a new jetty, and a ban on brawling on Sundays. The lanterns are done. The rest… pirates are difficult citizens.
textes.Mon punch, c'est ma fierté. Mais il me m: My punch is my pride and joy. But I'm short of coconuts: the boat from the jungle hasn't come.
textes.Mon père Ipi pêchait, mon grand-père pêc: My father Ipi fished, my grandfather fished, and his own father… we've already talked about him: he swam. Me, I was born on the riverbank, between two nets drying in the sun. My mother says I could hold a line before a spoon. Not true: first I held a fish. It was bigger than me, and it was the one that let go of me.
textes.Mon père a allumé un feu il y a cinquant: My father lit a fire fifty years ago and he's never let it go out. He always says you should think before you speak. Me, I hit before I think. We complement each other.
textes.Mon père a porté le courrier trente ans,: My father carried the post for thirty years, nose in the air. Now he counts the stars. I work by day, him by night. We cross paths at dusk. That's something.
textes.Mon père a sculpté la statue du roi Atla: My father carved the statue of King Atlas, up there, back when there was marble and sunshine. Under the sea, no more quarries: he switched to coral, grumbling. On my eighth birthday he gave me his silver chisel. “Red coral bites. Bite harder.” That's all I know about the trade. The rest, I made up.
textes.Mon père aimait la sardine bien noire, p: My father liked his sardines nice and black, almost burnt. Nobody grills them like that: it spoils the fish, they say. Mustapha does. Every time I pass, he puts one aside, at the edge of the embers, and lets it blacken. He doesn't ask. He knows. I eat it standing up, like my father.
textes.Mon père avait cinq ans quand l'île est: My father was five when the island went up. He was on the shoulders of Séraphin, his father, in the middle of the Esplanade. He told me a hundred times: the rumbling, the dust, the houses shaking, and then… the silence, and the sun. He used to say: “The silence lasted a minute, then everyone shouted for joy.” I was there too. In his story.
textes.Mon père bouche les trous de ce bateau,: My father plugs the holes in this ship, like his father before him. He sighs, he grumbles, he never says “I love you”. He says it with the crêpes he saves for me. I love him. That's exactly the problem.
textes.Mon père commandait la garde de la Skala: My father commanded the guard of the Skala. His father before him, the caïd Allal. As a child, I stole Si Larbi's fishing worms at the end of the jetty, and climbed on the cannons. The guards chased me off. I came back. Today, I'm the one chasing children off the cannons. They come back. That's the order of things.
textes.Mon père construisait des barques, en Br: My father built boats, in Brittany, in a little boatyard at the far end of an inlet. Fishing boats, sturdy, all the same. I drew three-masters in the sawdust with a stick. He used to say: “A fishing boat always comes back to port. A three-master leaves.” He was right. That's exactly why I wanted to build three-masters.
My father built rowing boats, in Brittany. I wanted to build ships. I left with the first one that came by. They were pirates. They needed a shipwright.
textes.Mon père coupait le papyrus dans les mar: My father cut papyrus in the marshes of the river mouth. He made sheets out of it and sold them to the scribes. Me, I wrote on them before they were sold, with a reed and soot: ibises, ducks, fish. My father scolded me, then he kept the sheets. He couldn't read. He said my ducks were very well written.
textes.Mon père cultivait un petit jardin derri: My father grew a little garden behind the house, squeezed between two walls. He grew more vegetables in it than there was room for. He gave me marks when I watered well. I got ten out of ten for watering and four for weeding. I never improved at weeding. Weeds have their charm.
textes.Mon père disait que j'ai tapé du pied av: My father said I tapped my foot before I could walk. My mother says I was already drumming in her belly.
textes.Mon père est mort il y a trois ans, {sur: My father died three years ago, {surnom}. That same week, the Petit Piston stopped. I've never started her again. Écrou thinks she's missing a part. Mostly she's missing the old man. I don't want to hear her run without him at the helm. I haven't told the girl. Don't tell her either. Let her sleep a little longer.
My father is a notary, on the mainland. As a little girl, I drew in the margins of his deeds while he saw his clients. One day, I illustrated a house sale with seagulls everywhere. Very good seagulls, they were. The client went to another notary. My father banned me from his office. I drew under the door.
textes.Mon père fabriquait des ressorts. Des pe: My father made springs. Small ones, big ones, watch springs and mattress springs. As a child, I sorted them by size, sitting on the floor, with Pistache, our old dog. He slept on the mattress springs and bounced as he dreamed. He was my best friend. I think Boulon looks a bit like him.
textes.Mon père gardait la Grande Porte avant m: My father guarded the Great Gate before me. I grew up in the guardhouse, between his spear and his mug. My first word was “Halt”. My mother wanted “mama”. She waited. The second was “Who goes there”. Hmph.
textes.Mon père gomme tout ce qu'il écrit. Moi,: My father rubs out everything he writes. I plant everything I touch. Mum used to say we were the two ends of the same pencil.
textes.Mon père m'a appelé Hapou, à cause de Ha: My father named me Hapou, after Hapy, the god of the flood. He thought it was funny. Every summer, when the river rose, the other children came to me: “Hapou, stop the flood, we want to play on the bank!” I said it had nothing to do with me. They didn't believe me. Forty years later, some of them still ask.
textes.Mon père m'a appris le tour : on le fait: My father taught me the wheel: you turn it with one hand and raise the jar with the other. And the secret of faience: fine sand, natron, a little copper for the blue. My first scarab looked like a bean. My father kept it. He said a scarab that looks like a bean is a scarab that's eaten well.
textes.Mon père m'a appris à marcher sans bruit: My father taught me to walk without a sound, to read tracks, to thank the animal you kill. You only take what you need.
textes.Mon père peignait les figures de proue,: My father painted figureheads, in a shipyard in the south: mermaids, lions, ladies with golden hair. I held his paint pots. At seven, I painted a moustache on a mermaid, on the sly. The ship sailed off with it. My father laughed for a week. He said I had the hand for it. And a funny sense of humour.
textes.Mon père portait des caisses sur le quai: My father carried crates on the quay. Me, I sat on the crates. I watched the boats leave. All day long. I said nothing. My mother said: “That boy has swallowed his tongue.” No. I was watching. The boats. The seagulls. Who goes out, who comes back. It came in handy.
textes.Mon père pêchait au filet sur le Lac de: My father fished with a net on the Lake of the Moon, at night. I grew up in his canoe. My cousin Tochtli too: our mothers are sisters. We were already fighting over the best spot, at the front. I won. He haggled to get it back. I still won. He said I understood nothing about trade. It was true.
textes.Mon père pêchait, ma mère ramendait les: My father fished, my mother mended the nets, and I followed old Mother Tréphine, the healer, at every low tide. She had me taste the seaweeds one by one: “This one heals, that one makes you sick, remember which.” I remembered. Especially that one.
textes.Mon père pêchait, mon grand-père pêchait: My father fished, my grandfather fished, and my grandfather's father… mostly swam. He fell out of the boat.
textes.Mon père pêchait, son père aussi, et com: My father fished, and his father too, and so on all the way back to the shipwreck. Before that they probably fished as well, just somewhere else. At five, I held the line while my father slept in the bottom of the boat. One day, I hauled up a conger eel bigger than me. I think it was the one that brought me back to shore.
textes.Mon père sonnait les cloches d'un petit: My father rang the bells of a little fishing port: noon, evening, storms, weddings. I'd climb the bell tower with him and sing over the bells, to see who'd win. The bells always won. But the seagulls came to listen to me. That's when I understood: I needed an instrument that didn't hurt people's ears.
textes.Mon père tenait La Rose des Vents avant: My father ran La Rose des Vents before me. I lived under the counter, among the atlases. In the afternoons, I'd take a piece of chalk and redraw his maps on the cobbles of the quay: the coasts, the capes, the bays. The fishermen walked over them laughing. In the evening, the port's brooms wiped everything away. The next day, I started again.
textes.Mon père tenait l'auberge avant moi. Ell: My father ran the inn before me. It was called “Le Mouton Tranquille” — the Quiet Sheep. One day, a giant frog came in through the door and sat down at a table. My father served it soup. It ate everything: the soup, the table, the tablecloth. We changed the name.
textes.Mon père tenait le Comptoir avant moi. I: My father ran the Trading Post before me. He wrote down in a notebook everything travellers told him about up top. “It's raining in Hautefond.” “The Grand Liftkeeper has a new apprentice.” “An island is floating above the clouds.” When he retired, he left me the notebook. I've filled six more. I still reread his pages in the evenings. His news is old. It's still true.
textes.Mon père tient une petite pension à Port: My father runs a little guesthouse in Port-Azur, with a terrace over the harbour. As a girl, I'd settle in a corner with my paints and paint the sea. Every day the same sea, the same polished blue, the same parasols. By fifteen, I'd painted it four hundred times. Guests would buy one before leaving. Me, I dreamed of another sea.
textes.Mon père tissait des voiles de bateau, s: My father wove boat sails, on the mainland. I wove with whatever I found: grass, wool threads, my own hair. He said I had spiders in my fingers. It was a compliment, I think.
textes.Mon père tressait les cordes des arcs, m: My father braided bowstrings, my mother sang so they would hold. When I was three, I plucked a bowstring and cried, because it played a very sad “A”. My father understood before I did: he carved me a little harp from a fallen branch. Five strings, and a lot of ambition.
My father wanted to make a sailor of me. I got seasick. He set me down on the quay with a bag of spices. He still tells that story laughing. So do I, now.
textes.Mon père était barde, mon grand-père aus: My father was a bard, and so was my grandfather. My great-grandfather sang for three kings. All three begged him to stop. But respectfully. It's a family tradition.
textes.Mon père était bûcheron, et son père aus: My father was a woodcutter, and his father too, and his father's father, right back to the first tree. We lived in a cabin at the edge of a forest so big you couldn't see the end of it. At seven, I carried the wood for winter. At ten, I carried my father when he'd eaten too much. Ha! We ate a lot, in my family. We were broad. Not fat. Broad.
textes.Mon père était calfat, mon grand-père au: My father was a caulker, so was my grandfather, and his before him, ever since the wreck. At seven, I was given my first job: holding the tar pot. I burnt three fingers on the first day. My father said: “Good. Now you know what's hot.” That was his whole lesson. It was a good lesson.
My father was a caulker, my grandfather too. My whole family has spent their lives keeping this ship from drowning. It's run aground, but it could still drown. It's a talent.
textes.Mon père était changeur à la Grande Hall: My father was a money-changer in the Great Hall. He weighed gold, I weighed my marbles. At four, I swallowed a ruby that was lying on his counter. The whole family waited three days. We got it back. Don't ask how. My father set it in my first belt buckle. I still wear it.
textes.Mon père était charbonnier. Il faisait l: My father was a charcoal burner. He made charcoal behind the ramparts, in pits that smoked day and night. I knew embers before I knew fish. At six, I could blow on a heap of ashes and bring a red ember back to life. My father said I had a blacksmith's lungs. Me, I just wanted to see the ember smile.
textes.Mon père était charpentier de marine. J': My father was a ship's carpenter. I grew up among hulls under repair, and I'd climb the masts the moment his back was turned. At six, I could tie a bowline, a clove hitch and a half hitch. Write my name, no. My mother used to say I had tar instead of blood. She wasn't wrong.
textes.Mon père était chasseur. Il m'a appris à: My father was a hunter. He taught me to walk without a sound, to read tracks, to thank the animal. At ten, I aimed at my first deer. He looked at me. I didn't shoot. My father said: “It wasn't your day. Nor his.” We went home with nothing. He was happy. Me too.
textes.Mon père était chauffeur sur la locomoti: My father was the fireman on the locomotive of the highlands line, the train that went up to fetch the shepherds' wool. I grew up on the tender, shovel in hand, throwing coal into the boiler and singing. One shovelful, one syllable. My father said I was the only fireman on the island who shovelled in rhyme.
textes.Mon père était chef d'une petite gare de: My father was the master of a little goods station, here, on the rusty rails. I grew up among wagons, points and oil cans. I could grease an axle before I could tie my shoelaces. In fact, I still don't tie them. I do a railwayman's knot.
textes.Mon père était chef de gare. Pas d'une v: My father was a stationmaster. Not of a real station: a goods yard, here, on the rusty rails. When it closed, he left me a toolbox and one sentence: “Anything that rolls can get going again.” People too, I think.
textes.Mon père était chiffonnier. Il ramassait: My father was a rag-and-bone man. He picked up everything that fell out of the workshops, and in Cliquetis, a lot falls out! I grew up in his cart, sitting on buckled wheels and spoutless teapots. My first treasure was a spring. It was good for nothing. It's still good for nothing. I've still got it, in my pocket. Here, look. Boing. Marvellous.
textes.Mon père était confiseur, mon ami, dans: My father was a confectioner, my friend, in a little town where nothing ever happened. Barley sugar, nougat, humbugs: I grew up among the jars. I sold his sweets to the neighbourhood children, and I made bets with them: heads, one humbug; tails, two. I always won. My father said I had a head for business. My mother said I had a two-headed coin.
textes.Mon père était cordonnier, au fond du so: My father was a cobbler, at the back of the souk. Our house had a low window, level with the street: from my bed, all I could see was feet. Thousands of feet. At seven, I could guess every passer-by's shoe size. At eight, I knew who they were just from their babouches. Faces, I discovered later. Less interesting.
textes.Mon père était docker sur le Vieux Bassi: My father was a docker on the Old Dock. At six, I brought him his packed lunch on the quays. At sixteen, I was carrying crates with him. The men laughed. After a week, they'd stopped laughing: I was carrying more than they were. They gave me a hook and a nickname: Barricade. Because nobody got past me.
textes.Mon père était docker, comme moi. Petit,: My father was a docker, like me. When I was little, I slept on the flour sacks while he unloaded the boats. It was soft, it smelled nice. When I wasn't sleeping, I counted seagulls. Once I counted forty-three. My father said: “Good. Now count the sacks.”
textes.Mon père était fermier, mon grand-père a: My father was a farmer, my grandfather too, and the turnips were already running away. My grandfather chased one all the way to the harbour. The turnip took a boat. We never saw it again. They say it started a family somewhere.
textes.Mon père était gardien de l'horloge de l: My father was keeper of the square's clock, and his father before him. As a little girl, I'd go up the tower with them and nap on the floor, my cheek against the frame of the mechanism. Tick, tock. I've never slept so well since. My mother said I had a pendulum instead of a heart. She wasn't entirely wrong.
textes.Mon père était guerrab, porteur d'eau du: My father was a guerrab, the souk's water carrier: a goatskin, copper cups at his belt, and a little bell so people could call him. I walked behind him with the clean cups. I grew up serving others their drinks. I never knew how to do anything else. I never wanted to.
textes.Mon père était guetteur avant moi, et so: My father was a lookout before me, and his father too. In our family, you're born with one eye on the horizon. At eight, my father hoisted me up to the main top and said: “Look. And say nothing until you're sure.” I looked. I've never talked much since.
textes.Mon père était l'allumeur de réverbères: My father was the lamplighter of Cliquetis. Every evening, I followed him with his long pole, from lamp to lamp, from the square down to the lower alleys. He touched a wick, and the street appeared. For a long time, I believed he was lighting the night itself, making it shine just for me. He laughed when I said so. He never really set me straight.
textes.Mon père était le boulanger d'Au Pain Do: My father was the baker at Au Pain Doré, and his father before him. I grew up in the bakehouse, up to my knees in flour. My father gave me the rolls that went wrong, and I practised pointing in the yard, with a loaf for the jack. At ten, I could land a stale roll a finger's width from the loaf. The neighbourhood dogs adored me.
textes.Mon père était pochtecatl, marchand voya: My father was a pochtecatl, a travelling merchant. He'd leave for months with his staff and his porters, loaded with feathers, jade, cacao. I waited for him at the end of the causeway, every evening. When he came back, he'd empty his bags onto the mat, and he'd tell stories. The stories were worth more than the jade. He still says so. He's eighty, and he's still telling them.
My father was a pochtecatl, a travelling merchant. He'd be gone for months, loaded with feathers, jade, cacao. He came back with stories. Me, I stay at the tianguis. The stories come to me.
textes.Mon père était potier, son père aussi. À: My father was a potter, and his father too. At six, I modelled a faience hippo. My father fired it in the big oven, with his jars. It came out blue, all blue, with one eye higher than the other. It's still on my shelf. I call it Gros-Bleu. It's my best work. Don't tell the customers.
textes.Mon père était pêcheur de fardines, fur: My father wath a thardine fitherman, on a little ithland in the thouth. He had all hith teeth, he did, and he whithtled like a blackbird ath he hauled in hith netth. Me, I wath the thmallest of theven kidth. We ate fith in the morning, fith at noon, and in the evening… potatoeth, for a change. Good timeth, friend.
textes.Mon père était pêcheur sur ce lac, et so: My father was a fisherman on this lake, and so was his father. When my father got too old, he gave me his boat and said: “Are you scared, son? Then fish with your fear. It'll make you careful.” I've been scared for forty years. I've never lost a single finger. Fear is the best fishing rod there is.
textes.Mon père était pêcheur, et il chantait e: My father was a fisherman, and he sang at sea. The whole fleet heard him before they saw his boat. When he came back, he'd sit on the quay with his oud, and the neighbours brought out their chairs. I inherited both: the singing and the oud. And the voice, too. Especially the voice, according to the neighbours.
textes.Mon père était pêcheur, et son père auss: My father was a fisherman, and his father too. The first time he took me to sea, I was seven. He showed me the two lighthouses: “Green on the left, red on the right, and you always come home.” When we got back, my grandmother Zahra was waiting under the arcades. She looked at my three sardines, then at me, and she said: “Good eye. Both of them.”
textes.Mon père était pêcheur, mon grand-père a: My father was a fisherman, so was my grandfather, and his father before him, on this very beach. At four, I slept at the bottom of the boat, between the lobster pots. I knew the names of the fish before I knew my letters. Even today, I read the sea better than a book. Yep.
textes.Mon père était pêcheur. Il disait : « Ce: My father was a fisherman. He used to say: “He who talks scares the fish away.” So on board, we didn't talk. Not in the evening either. We watched the sea. I learned to listen before I learned to talk. It stuck.
textes.Mon père était relieur, dans une petite: My father was a bookbinder, in a small town in the south whose name would mean nothing to you. I grew up with the smell of glue and leather. At six, I fell off a ladder in his workshop, a dictionary in my arms. I broke my arm; the dictionary, nothing. That day I understood which of us was the sturdier. And I became afraid of ladders.
textes.Mon père était savetier, près de la port: My father was a cobbler, near the north gate. At six, I used to steal his awls to pierce the grocer's old iron tins. I'd put a candle inside, and the wall of our room would fill with little suns. My father would sigh: “This boy will be making holes all his life.” He was right. He just didn't think it would become a trade.
textes.Mon père était scaphandrier. Petite, je: My father was a deep-sea diver. When I was little, I helped him close his helmet: twelve nuts, in order, crosswise. I counted them out loud. He'd say: “If you forget one, I'll know straight away.” I never forgot a single one. Not that day, nor since.
textes.Mon père était scaphandrier. Quand j'éta: My father was a deep-sea diver. When I was little, I helped him close his helmet: twelve bolts, in order, crosswise. I counted them out loud. He used to say: “If you forget one, I'll know straight away.” I never forgot a single one. Today, I still count out loud. People think I'm talking to myself. I'm talking to my father.
textes.Mon père était sergent de la garde. Il m: My father was a sergeant in the guard. He woke me up with a bugle, even on Sundays. At eight, I made my bed with hospital corners and saluted the cat. My mother used to say: “That child has never run in his life.” Not true. I ran. In step.
textes.Mon père était soudeur sur un chantier n: My father was a welder at a shipyard. As a kid, I'd watch the sparks through the workshop door, the way other kids watch fireworks. He gave me my first welding goggles when I was twelve. Too big. I saw everything in green. I never gave them back.
My father was a typesetter at the Academy. I learned to read backwards, in the lead type cases, long before I could read the right way round! My first article, at eight, was one line long: “Neighbour's cat eats a spring.” A total exclusive. The cat was perfectly fine, thank you. It just bounced a bit, that's all.
textes.Mon père était un baron sévère, toujours: My father was a stern baron, always bareheaded, even in a hailstorm. At five, I wore a little straw hat I'd found at the market. He hated it. The day he died, I opened his wardrobe: there was only one hat inside. Mine. The one from when I was five. Since then, I've worn one every day.
textes.Mon père était un grand baron, sérieux,: My father was a great baron, serious, stern, always bareheaded. When he died, I found a single hat in his wardrobe: a child's little straw hat. Mine, from when I was five. He had kept it. Since then, I wear hats.
textes.Mon père, Ambroise Lisse, m'emmenait sur: My father, Ambroise Lisse, used to take me to the quays of the Old Dock to count crates. He said counting was what mattered most. I preferred carrying oranges with a very strong lady docker who laughed all the time. She gave me a toffee one evening. My father said it wasn't profitable.
textes.Mon père, Firmin, était croupier, et son: My father, Firmin, was a croupier, and his father before him. I learned to count with chips instead of pebbles, and to shuffle cards before I could tie my shoes. My father used to say: “A croupier doesn't smile, doesn't sweat, doesn't lose his temper.” At eight, I had already stopped smiling. My mother found it sad. I found it professional.
textes.Mon père, Thrain le Lent, quarante et un: My father, Thrain the Slow, forty-first king, wanted to teach me to rule. Me, I wanted to hide in the cellar of the Blazing Mug, behind the biggest barrel. A young innkeeper found me there one evening. Ulfa. She didn't give me away. She taught me to pull a fizz. A king never forgets.
textes.Mon père, Tobias, bouche les trous du ba: My father, Tobias, plugs the holes in the ship. My mother, Annaig, used to sew its sails. I grew up between the two, with tar on one cheek and thread on the other. My mother said I was a well-caulked sail. I never knew if it was a compliment. I think it was.
textes.Mon père, c'est Augustin, l'ancien maîtr: My father is Augustin, the old schoolmaster. He rubs out everything he writes. That's why our name is Gomme: eraser. Me, I don't rub anything out: I plant.
textes.Mon père, c'est Tilleul. Il a pris tous: My father is Tilleul. He took all the family's words. I took the hammer. As a cub, during his stories, I banged on pots. Bing. Bang. It helped him, he said. At ten, old Charbon, the bears' blacksmith, took me on as an apprentice. He didn't talk much. We got on well.
textes.Mon père, c'est le Capitaine Charbonnel,: My father is Captain Charbonnel, the harbour master. He wanted me to sail. I get seasick. So I did the opposite: I stay on the quay, and the ships bring me my spices from the far end of the archipelago.
textes.Mon père, il fait toutes les barques du: My dad makes every boat in the port with his hands. His hands are the strongest in the world. But wood takes ages. Sooo long. I want boats that go fast.
My father. He talks for two. For ten. You want to talk, talk to Tilleul. Me, I listen. I love him. Don't repeat that to him.
textes.Mon père. Il pêche, je vends. Il jure qu: My father. He fishes, I sell. He swears he's seen the Pond King. I think he dreamt it. And it worries me, watching him spend his life on that jetty.
textes.Mon péché mignon ? %s. Rien qu'en y pens: My guilty pleasure? %s. Just thinking about it makes me smile.
textes.Mon record tient toujours, Pépin ?: Is my record still standing, Pépin?
textes.Mon record, je l'ai fait un mardi, à sei: I set my high score on a Tuesday, at 4:12 pm. It was raining. There were three people in the Arcade. When I beat the final dragon, everyone screamed. Even the attendant. He never screams.
textes.Mon rire ? C'est un outil. Sous terre, q: My laugh? It's a tool. Underground, when there's noise everywhere, a good laugh carries all the way to the bottom of the mine. Ludovic says it's his best alarm: as long as he hears it, all is well.
textes.Mon rire, on l'entend depuis le Mât des: You can hear my laugh from the Airship Mast. Captain Héloïse says she uses it to find her way in fog. “Straight ahead, towards Rosalie's laugh.” I find that very flattering.
textes.Mon rival ! Approche, si tu l'oses !: My rival! Come closer, if you dare!
textes.Mon rival ! Te voilà enfin ! J'ai battu: My rival! There you are at last! I beat three more slimes than you this week. I think. I didn't count yours. But I can feel it.
textes.Mon rouge ! J'ai pensé à vous en broyant: My red! I thought of you while grinding my colours. Hibiscus turns brown: you're worth more than hibiscus.
textes.Mon rêve ? Acheter la Chaumière des Glyc: My dream? To buy the Wisteria Cottage. With my hundred and forty coins and a lot of patience. I'd put up a shelf in it for my failures. It'll need to be a big shelf.
My dream? To put shoes on the pirate captain. He's been wearing boots for thirty years. Imagine the smell.
textes.Mon rêve ? Crier une nouvelle si belle q: My dream? To shout news so wonderful that the whole island hears it at once. From the harbour to the Fangs. And all the frogs dive in together, for joy.
textes.Mon rêve ? Dire ma phrase à Honorine. Un: My dream? To say my sentence to Honorine. Just once. And for her not to laugh. Or to laugh, but kindly. And afterwards, to catch my breath for real.
textes.Mon rêve ? Entrer dans le Cœur-de-Pierre: My dream? To get inside Stoneheart and draw what's in there. First you'd have to open the gate. And for that…
textes.Mon rêve ? Faire le tour de l'archipel e: My dream? To sail round the archipelago. The village, the jungle, the elves' island, the dwarves' mountain… they even say there's an island that flies.
textes.Mon rêve ? Finir un sermon. Un seul. Du: My dream? To finish a sermon. Just one. From beginning to end, without falling asleep. I don't hold out much hope. But the Dawn loves difficult dreams.
textes.Mon rêve ? Forger l'épée d'un héros de r: My dream? To forge the sword of a rank S hero. A blade people will talk about in a hundred years. And to hear someone say, at the end of the world: “That one's a Brunehaut.”
textes.Mon rêve ? Gagner encore le concours du: My dream? To win the finest turnip contest again. Without paint. Well, without “enhancement”. Just to see Germaine's face. And then share the prize with her. Maybe.
textes.Mon rêve ? Je n'y ai jamais vraiment pen: My dream? I've never really thought about it.
textes.Mon rêve ? LA tenue d'aventurier parfait: My dream? THE perfect adventurer's outfit. Sturdy, pretty, doesn't stick to jelly, doesn't catch fire, and with one more pocket. There's always a pocket missing.
textes.Mon rêve ? Lancer un éclair, un seul, qu: My dream? To cast one lightning bolt, just one, that goes exactly where I aim it. And then stand there, hair nice and flat, watching it go.
textes.Mon rêve ? Marcher d'un bout à l'autre d: My dream? To walk from one end of the Great Square to the other without falling. Just once. With everyone watching. And clap for myself at the end.
textes.Mon rêve ? Ouvrir une paillote sur chaqu: My dream? Open a beach hut on every island. Even at the dwarves'. Especially at the dwarves', they're thirsty.
textes.Mon rêve ? Pêcher une journée entière sa: My dream? To fish for a whole day without being scared. Just one. Feet in the water, sun on my back, and not a frog in sight. I think I'd fall asleep. Like Gilles.
textes.Mon rêve ? Qu'on raconte encore mes hist: My dream? That people will still tell my stories in a hundred years, on this very bench. Not under my name. Just the stories. Names wear out. Stories grow.
textes.Mon rêve ? Que plus personne n'ait faim: My dream? That nobody in Montjoie goes hungry anymore. Ever. Not the adventurers, not the guards, not the goblins. Well, the goblins, I'm not sure. But the others, yes.
textes.Mon rêve ? Redescendre une fois. Jusqu'a: My dream? To go back down once. To the third floor. With Hugues in front, not panicking, and me behind, with the packed lunch. Like before. My knees can say what they like.
textes.Mon rêve ? Savoir qui a déposé les sacs: My dream? To find out who left the sacks of seeds. To hug them, say thank you, and make them a soup. Even if it's someone I don't like. Especially if it's someone I don't like.
textes.Mon rêve ? Trouver enfin, dans tout ce b: My dream? To finally find, in all this clutter, one object that's really, truly magic. Just one! And not remember buying it. What a surprise that would be!
textes.Mon rêve ? Trouver la vingt et unième re: My dream? To find the twenty-first frog recipe. The one that will beat Rissole's pie. And to see Master Hugues finally choose. That would end a thirty-year war.
textes.Mon rêve ? Un bal des chapeaux ! Toute l: My dream? A hat ball! The whole town, each with the most extravagant hat possible. And I wouldn't even be the most ridiculous. Well, yes I would. But only just.
textes.Mon rêve ? Un dernier grand voyage, auto: My dream? One last great voyage, around the whole archipelago, with Albertine on my shoulder. And to come back in time to see the lighthouse light up. My lighthouse. My home.
textes.Mon rêve ? Un duel. Le grand duel. Toi e: My dream? A duel. The great duel. You and me, at the top of the Fangs, in a thunderstorm, in front of the whole town. And afterwards… a meal. Together. Rivals get hungry too.
textes.Mon rêve ? Un dîner parfait. Un seul. Sa: My dream? A perfect dinner. Just one. No rockets, no shouting under the windows, no train caught on my horns. The cutlery aligned, the guests on time, and Her Highness laughing. The laughter, I shall tolerate.
textes.Mon rêve ? Un exploit vrai. Un seul ! Av: My dream? A true great deed. Just one! With witnesses, sunshine and not a single wisp of fog. And then, to write to my father: “I saved someone.”
textes.Mon rêve ? Un grand banquet sur la Grand: My dream? A great banquet on the Great Square, with all of Montjoie, and bread for everyone. And Noisette running between the tables. And someone coming back from the sea, just in time for dessert.
textes.Mon rêve ? Un lit à côté de la Porte Nor: My dream? A bed next to the North Gate. That way, I'd be on guard and rested at the same time. The Captain says it's against article twelve. I think it would make him jealous.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une Guilde où toutes les fich: My dream? A Guild where every record is up to date, every contract handed in, and every adventurer home for dinner. Just one day like that. I'd file it under “Perfect”.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une ballade si belle que même: My dream? A ballad so beautiful that even Mélusine would forget to ring her bell. And the Baron would take off his hat. All his hats.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une journée entière sans que: My dream? A whole day without anyone knocking on my office door. I wouldn't know what to do. I think I'd tidy up. But for fun.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une journée sans alerte. Une: My dream? One day without an alert. Just one. I'd do a quiet patrol, I'd drink a hot coffee, and I wouldn't run. It would be very strange. I think I'd be bored.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une machine qui pense. Le pro: My dream? A machine that thinks. Professor Boum says he has one. It exploded last week.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une potion de soin parfaite,: My dream? A perfect healing potion, with no side effects at all. None! Not even a little colour change. I'll taste it, and I'll stay the same colour. What a triumph.
textes.Mon rêve ? Une récolte de navets qui ne: My dream? A turnip harvest that doesn't run away. Just one. I wouldn't know what to do with myself. I think I'd be bored. All right, let's say: a harvest that runs away more slowly.
textes.Mon rêve ? Vendre la Chaumière à quelqu': My dream? To sell the Cottage to someone good, and walk past one evening and see the window lit. And say nothing. Just wax my moustache, and smile.
textes.Mon rêve ? Voir un aventurier de Montjoi: My dream? To see an adventurer from Montjoie reach rank S. A real one. I'll cry so much that Mamie Rissole will have to wring out my beard.
textes.Mon rêve ? Être rang S ! Comme Maître Hu: My dream? To be rank S! Like Master Hugues, but without crying. Well, maybe a little. And to forge my own rank S sword. With Mum watching.
textes.Mon rêve ? Être réceptionniste de la Gui: My dream? To be the Guild receptionist, like Églantine. With a stamp. I'd stamp all the cards. And people's hands. And maybe the frogs.
textes.Mon rêve, c'est de faire le tour du mond: My dream is to go round the world by air. Without stopping. Just looking at everything, from above. I know I'll come back to Hautefond all the same. You always come back to where someone's waiting for you with a hot chocolate.
textes.Mon rêve, c'est de manger une glace sur: My dream is to eat an ice cream on a beach. A real beach, with sand that warms your feet and waves that tickle. Up here we have sunshine all the time, but no sand. And Gustave makes his ice cream out of cloud. It's not the same.
textes.Mon rêve, c'est que tout l'archipel vien: My dream is for the whole archipelago to come and dance in our Great Square one day. We demons have a bad reputation. Because of the horns, no doubt. Or the smoke.
textes.Mon sabre corsaire, je le forge comme ma: I forge my corsair sabre the way my grandmother made pie: hitting hard and singing off-key.
textes.Mon salon est dans le quartier des Artis: My salon is in the Artisans' Quarter, west of the Lower Town, between Grisette's workshop and Zigomar's. On one side, they criticise my collars; on the other, they blow things up. It's a very stimulating neighbourhood.
textes.Mon sauveur ! Mon héros ! Mon Fernand !: My saviour! My hero! My Fernand!
textes.Mon sauveur ! Écoute, ce soir je joue «: My saviour! Listen, tonight I'm playing “The Azur Waltz” just for you.
textes.Mon secret ? Le champignon de braise. Il: My secret? The ember mushroom. It grows in the hot ash, near the fumaroles. It tingles, it warms, it heals.
textes.Mon secret ? Le miel sauvage. Les abeill: My secret? Wild honey. The bees of Bois-Doré feed on the Mother Tree: their honey is golden like its leaves.
textes.Mon secret ? Une goutte de miel des elfe: My secret? A drop of elf honey in the dough. Shh.
textes.Mon secret, {surnom} ? Je fais toujours: My secret, {surnom}? I always make one plate too many. Always. Because there's always someone who turns up late, someone who didn't dare come, someone who's had a bad day. That plate is the most important one. Today, maybe it was yours.
textes.Mon serré, Gisèle ! Le meilleur de l'arc: My short black, Gisèle! The best in the archipelago!
textes.Mon serré, Gisèle ! Le plus serré de l'a: My espresso, Gisèle! The strongest in the archipelago!
textes.Mon soufflet a un trou. Mon apprenti a u: My bellows have a hole. My apprentice has a hole in his head. Everything's leaking today.
textes.Mon sérieux préféré ! Toi qui dis tout f: My favourite straight face! You who say everything frankly: tell me frankly, do I look serious right now?
textes.Mon tajine de poisson est célèbre jusqu': My fish tajine is famous all the way to Carène. The pirates order three pots a week from me. They eat like whales.
textes.Mon tampon s'appelle Clac. Oui, il a un: My stamp is called Clac. Yes, it has a name. It has stamped every adventurer's card in Montjoie for eight years. It's a bit worn on the left side, because I stamp with enthusiasm.
textes.Mon trésor de braise ! (Elle serre Pépin: My ember treasure! (She hugs Pépin so tight that his little horns turn red.) You, you come back to the market whenever you like: the chili peppers are yours, for life. Well, these ones. Here.
textes.Mon trésor à moi, je l'ai enterré sous l: My very own treasure, I buried it under the sandcastle. It's a shell, a marble and a dry noodle. Don't tell anyone. Especially not the seagulls.
textes.Mon uniforme, Colombe me l'a rapporté de: My uniform, Colombe brought it back for me from the big island, four years ago. She told me she'd bought it at a market. It fitted me perfectly, as if it had been made for me. It has never come unstitched. I have never found a market that sells things so well made. She was lucky.
textes.Mon usine, l'Usine Grise, est au sud-est: My factory, the Grey Factory, is to the south-east, behind the Spore Wood. Five floors underground: offices, an assembly line, a boiler room, a warehouse, and at the very bottom… No. That's confidential. Don't go down there. Whatever you do, don't go down there.
textes.Mon vieil ami ! Assieds-toi, enfin… il n: My old friend! Have a seat, well… there's no chair. Have a seat standing up.
textes.Mon village est à l'est, derrière la Sal: My village is to the east, behind the Bell Hall! Listen to the melody at the lectern, then play it again on the bells.
textes.Mon violon est en bois de cendre, avec d: My violin is made of ash wood, with strings of hellhound hair. Flammèche saves it for me when she brushes her puppies. It sounds warm, a little husky, like a cat purring by the fire.
textes.Mon voyageur du village ! Votre petite c: My traveller from the village! Your little cross is still on my map. It seems to be doing very well.
textes.Mon voyageur venu de la mer ! Votre peti: My traveller from the sea! Your little wave is still in the corner of my map. With its question mark.
textes.Mon école était sur une passerelle, entr: My school was on a walkway, between the Eraser Oak and the Blotter Oak. The pupils sat on the planks with their legs dangling. Nobody ever dropped anything, except erasers. There are erasers all over the grass underneath.
textes.Mon électricité vient du vent et du sole: My electricity comes from the wind and the sun: wind turbines made from old fans on the roof of the Spinning Mill, and panels salvaged from the Scrapyard. And when there's no wind and no sun, Tapage pedals on a dynamo bike. He says it's his sport.
textes.Mon élève du « un peu » ! Alors, ce nœud: My “a little” pupil! So, that knot? Under, over, and pull tight. Not too tight.
textes.Mon élève qui danse « plutôt bien » ! Le: My pupil who dances “pretty well”! The cat's waiting for you on the square. He wants to see your crab.
textes.Mon élève qui savait que la tomate est u: My pupil who knew the tomato is a fruit! Ten out of ten, it's written in my notebook. You're top of my class.
textes.Mon épouvantail, au milieu des prés, s'a: My scarecrow, in the middle of the meadows, is called Mister Paille. He doesn't frighten anyone. The crows sit on his arms for a chat.
textes.Mon épée d'acier. Trois semaines de forg: My steel sword. Three weeks at the forge, tempered in seawater. Hold it tight: it's my masterpiece. Don't let it rust.
textes.Mon épée s'appelle Crépuscule. Je l'ai b: My sword is called Twilight. I named it myself, on the cliff, at sunset. I gave a long speech. Then I slipped, and spent the night on the cliff. But the name stuck.
textes.Mon épée te va bien. Évidemment : c'est: My sword suits you. Of course it does: I forged it.
textes.Mon épée, c'est pour les combats qui vie: My sword is for the fights to come. Strange things happen at night in the jungle, {surnom}. Train on my dummies downstairs: three hits in a row, and the last one hurts.
textes.Mon étal ? Pommes, baies, et le miel de: My stall? Apples, berries, and forest honey, which Pomme-de-Pin climbs right to the top to fetch. I pay her in coins, obviously. I live with Lilas in the pond tree, and in the evening I dance behind her at the Circle. And between customers, I make fun of Bondi's three carrots. That's free. The only free thing on my stall.
textes.Mon étal est au Grand Marché, au nord-es: My stall is at the Great Market, in the north-east of the Lower Town. Follow the smell of brioche. If you smell chili, that's Zébuline: too far left. If you hear sneezing, that's Kraxx: too far right.
textes.Mon étal est sur la Grand-Place du March: My stall is on the Great Market Square, next to the fountain. The best spot in Montjoie. Monsieur Prosper wanted to buy it from me to put in a “prestige boutique”. I offered him an apple. He left. With the apple.
Mr Altaïr. The Column salutes you.
textes.Monsieur Anatole, elle arrive quand, la: Mr Anatole, when's the next cabin coming?
textes.Monsieur Asmodin ! J'ai une nouvelle inv: Monsieur Asmodin! I have a new invention for the palace!
textes.Monsieur Asmodin ! Lundi, neuf heures, c: Monsieur Asmodin! Monday, nine o'clock, as always!
textes.Monsieur Asmodin ! Vingt brioches, toute: Monsieur Asmodin! Twenty brioches, all straight!
textes.Monsieur Aubin ! Merci encore pour les é: Monsieur Aubin! Thanks again for the stars.
textes.Monsieur Aubin m'a fait onze potions con: Monsieur Aubin has made me eleven potions against lightning. None of them worked. But I've been blue, green, orange and polka-dotted. He takes notes. He's very serious. And very colourful.
textes.Monsieur Aubin m'a fait une nouvelle pot: Monsieur Aubin made me a new potion. I don't dare drink it. It's polka-dotted.
textes.Monsieur Aubin m'a fait une potion contr: Monsieur Aubin made me an anti-lightning potion. I stayed blue for a whole day. The lightning didn't notice the difference.
textes.Monsieur Aubin m'a fait une potion pour: Monsieur Aubin made me a potion to stay awake. I slept for two days. It was wonderful. Then he made me another one, and I saw all the stars. That was wonderful too.
textes.Monsieur Bobor fait les meilleures brioc: Monsieur Bobor makes the best brioches in Pandémonia. He is as round as his brioches and almost as warm. I suspect him of botching one brioche a day, on purpose, to see my face.
textes.Monsieur Bobor. Vingt brioches. Droites,: Monsieur Bobor. Twenty brioches. Straight, if you please.
textes.Monsieur Brasero, je souhaiterais dire q: Mr Brasero, I would like to say a few words.
Mr Bévue. Hands on the table.
textes.Monsieur Cinq-Doigts est le Fournisseur: Monsieur Cinq-Doigts is the Official Supplier to the City, by decree. He sold me my governor's chain and my golden tricorn. He accepts payment in promises. He's a man of the future.
Mr Clou… thank you for the metronome.
textes.Monsieur Cogne cherche un engrenage. Gon: Mr Cogne is looking for a gear. Gonzague, at the port, saw something golden near the crane. I added the two together.
textes.Monsieur Cogne est très gentil et très t: Mr Cogne is very kind and very stubborn. His engine can't run forever. I know it. I'll never tell him. Some calculations you keep to yourself.
textes.Monsieur Crochet ne parle pas, ne triche: Monsieur Crochet doesn't talk, doesn't cheat, and keeps his hook under my table when I ask him to. He's the most restful player at the Shark's Tooth. I appreciate him.
textes.Monsieur Crochet. Sous la table, je vous: Mister Crochet. Under the table, if you please.
textes.Monsieur Edmond ! Il a encore ronflé, ce: Monsieur Edmond! He was snoring again last night, on the fourth floor!
textes.Monsieur Edmond, c'est trente ans de réc: Monsieur Edmond is thirty years at reception and a moustache trimmed to the millimetre. He taught me everything. He says I talk too much. He doesn't talk enough, so it balances out.
textes.Monsieur Fil sourit trop. Ses programmes: Mr Fil smiles too much. So do his programs. I found something hidden in one of them. I don't know what it is yet. But I'll find out.
textes.Monsieur Fil, le marchand au chapeau, de: Monsieur Fil, the merchant with the hat, two streets away… I don't like his programs. Last week I fixed three cleaning robots that had installed one. They were doing the housework… at the neighbours'.
textes.Monsieur Fil, le marchand au chapeau… Se: Monsieur Fil, the merchant with the hat… His programs hide things. I don't know what yet. Do me a favour: if he offers you something “cheap”, think twice. Three times, even.
textes.Monsieur Fil, le marchand de programmes: Mr Fil, the program seller of the Alleys, sold you his "Turbo-Adventure 3000" for a few coins. He copied it into your travel journal… and it was a virus! A fake one, luckily: it's part of the game. Glitch, the Arcade District hacker, is helping you get rid of it.
textes.Monsieur Fil, votre programme était un v: Monsieur Fil, your program was a virus!
textes.Monsieur Fusain, votre Mur est-il… à l'é: Mr Fusain, is your Wall… to scale?
textes.Monsieur Gaspard dit qu'une montre, ça s: Mr Gaspard says you have to listen to a watch before you mend it.
textes.Monsieur Gaspard l'horloger me donne les: Mister Gaspard the clockmaker gives me the gears that are too small. He says they're “out of tolerance”. Me, I tolerate them just fine.
textes.Monsieur Gustave ! J'ai besoin de la cav: Monsieur Gustave! I need the cellar, just a little.
textes.Monsieur Gustave, c'est le meilleur alch: Monsieur Gustave is the best alchemist in the world, and he says so himself. He lends me his cellar. He shouts a bit when it smokes, but he shouts with a smile. He tells everyone I'm gifted.
textes.Monsieur Hulotte ! Vous voyez mon museau: Mister Hulotte! Can you see my snout?
textes.Monsieur Hulotte, il voit dans le noir,: Mister Hulotte can see in the dark, and he counts all the stars. He climbs the stairs really slowly, so I climb with him. He says I ask too many questions. He answers anyway.
textes.Monsieur Lisse a fait repeindre en gris: Mr Lisse had the wall behind his office painted grey. Grey! The wall was begging me. I heard it. Tonight, it'll have flowers.
textes.Monsieur Lisse a gardé dans son tiroir u: Monsieur Lisse keeps a photo in his drawer of a pallet hut, built by a little boy. Him. I saw it while filing. I didn't file anything. Some things can't be filed away.
textes.Monsieur Lisse est un homme très gris, a: Mr Lisse is a very grey man, with a pallet hut in a drawer. I've worked for him for eight years. I think he's better than he thinks.
textes.Monsieur Lisse est venu manger une fois,: Mr Lisse came to eat once, in disguise. He asked for “the optimised menu”. I served him a soup and a smile. He finished the soup. He left ten coins. He never told anyone.
textes.Monsieur Lisse m'a proposé d'acheter la: Mr Lisse offered to buy the radio. He wanted to call it “Lisse FM, the optimised radio”. I said no, live on air. A thousand listeners applauded. And three seagulls.
textes.Monsieur Lisse range ses panneaux « BIEN: Monsieur Lisse is packing away his “COMING SOON” signs. He looks at the Hall. He taps his foot. In rhythm.
textes.Monsieur Lisse repeint tout en gris. Je: Mr Lisse paints everything grey. I paint everything in colour. It's the most colourful war in the archipelago, and I fully intend to win it.
textes.Monsieur Lisse veut tout raser pour cons: Mr Lisse wants to flatten everything to build his “Lisse-Center”. An eternal shopping mall. Eternal! Just thinking about it makes my ears hurt. And my ears have been through a lot.
textes.Monsieur Lisse voulait couper mon saule: Mister Lisse wanted to cut down my willow and raze my wood. I fight him with all my might. But for three hundred days, he came to say good morning at the foot of the tree. It's complicated.
textes.Monsieur Lisse voulait racheter ma radio: Mr Lisse wanted to buy my radio and turn it into “Lisse FM”. I said no, live on air. But I suspect he listens every night. In secret.
textes.Monsieur Lisse, votre rendez-vous de qui: Mr Lisse, your three o'clock appointment.
textes.Monsieur Lumen est un homme charmant, sa: Mr Lumen is a charming man, learned, luminous, and the worst borrower on the island after Mr Fiole. He returns books. Always. Years late and with notes in the margins.
textes.Monsieur Lunette est mon ministre de la: Monsieur Lunette is my Minister of Geography. He doesn't quite know it, but he accepted the plaque. He drew the most beautiful map of Port-Coutelas ever made.
textes.Monsieur Malaterre ! Notre traité tient: Monsieur Malaterre! Is our treaty still holding?
textes.Monsieur Malaterre m'a gagné aux dés. Mo: Monsieur Malaterre won me at dice. Me! The Governor! For three days, I polished his boots. He calls it a game. I call it a state visit. We disagree.
textes.Monsieur Malaterre sourit avec vingt-deu: Monsieur Malaterre smiles with twenty-two carats and cheats with the rest. He knows it, I know it. At my table, he plays honest. It costs him dearly. It's a pleasure to watch him lose.
textes.Monsieur Malaterre. Vos manches sont bie: Monsieur Malaterre. Are your sleeves properly sewn up?
Mr Pascal said “Quieter!” So we run quieter. But faster.
textes.Monsieur Pascal a encore écrit une récla: Mr Pascal has written another complaint. Against the wind, this time. He says it blows too hard on his newspaper.
textes.Monsieur Pascal a écrit sa quarantième r: Mr Pascal has written his fortieth complaint about the music from down below. He taps out the beat while he writes it.
textes.Monsieur Pascal commande une chouquette: Mr Pascal orders a choux bun every morning. He eats half; the other half goes in his pocket for the sparrows. I slip him an extra one on the sly. He pretends not to notice. We get on wonderfully, without ever saying so.
textes.Monsieur Pascal commande une chouquette,: Mr Pascal orders one sugar puff, just one, every morning. He eats half. The other half goes in his pocket. I know where it goes: to the sparrows at the Residences. He doesn't know I know. I slip him an extra one on the sly.
textes.Monsieur Pascal dit que mes couchers de: Mr Pascal says my sunsets are “too orange”. He comes to check every evening, at the Belvedere. He stays till the end. He says: “That one'll do.” Coming from him, it's a triumph. I keep his “that'll do”s in a notebook. I have forty-two.
textes.Monsieur Pascal fait semblant d'être gro: Mr Pascal pretends to be grumpy, but I saw him feeding crumbs to the sparrows behind the Residences. He told me: “You didn't see anything.” I said: “OK.” But I saw everything.
textes.Monsieur Pascal m'a dit que mes couchers: Mr Pascal told me my sunsets were “too orange”. The next day, he came to the Belvedere to check. He stayed until the very end. He said: “Fine. That one will do.” It was an enormous compliment.
textes.Monsieur Pascal nourrit les moineaux der: Mr Pascal feeds the sparrows behind the Residences, every morning at four minutes past seven. He asked me not to say so. I did not say so. I only observed it out loud. That is not the same. I think.
textes.Monsieur Pascal s'est posé sur toi… D'ha: Mr Pascal has landed on you… He doesn't usually land on anyone. Here, very quietly: some honey from the High-Altitude Greenhouses. Flora Verdine brings us some when she comes to see her former lodgers.
Mr Pascal has landed on you… He doesn't usually land on anyone. Here, very quietly: a bag of sunflower seeds, my little girl's snack. She won't mind.
Mr Pascal has landed on you… He doesn't usually land on anyone. Here, very quietly: a bag of sunflower seeds, my little boy's snack. He won't mind.
textes.Monsieur Pascal se plaint des gens du Pl: Mr Pascal complains about the Floor folk queuing at the Station. But every morning he comes and sits on the bench to watch the queue. “To keep an eye on things,” he says. He smiles when the children go “wow”. I've seen him.
textes.Monsieur Pascal se plaint que je passe a: Mr Pascal complains that I fly over his balcony. I never fly over his balcony. I fly over his sparrows. He feeds them in secret, every morning. I see him from above. He doesn't know. It's my favourite secret on the island.
Mr Pascal complains that I fly over his balcony. I never fly over his balcony. I fly over his sparrows. He feeds them, in secret. I can see him from up above. He doesn't know.
textes.Monsieur Pascal vient se plaindre chaque: Mr Pascal comes every week to complain that the island is tilting. I measure. It isn't tilting. He says: “Then it's me who's tilting.” I pour him a tea. He tilts less. He was an excellent pressure engineer. Mostly he comes to talk engines. He'll never admit it.
Mr Pascal comes to complain every week that the island is “leaning towards the Floor”. I measure. It isn't leaning. He says: “Then it's me who's leaning.” I pour him a tea. He leans less.
textes.Monsieur Pascal vote contre tout, puis i: Mr Pascal votes against everything, then comes back with a good idea. The birdhouse in the Greenhouses: that was him. The benches at the Station: him again. He says all he does is complain. He does a lot more than that.
textes.Monsieur Pascal, de la Cité des Nuées, n: Mr Pascal, from the City of Clouds, sent us a box of choux buns, with a note: “For the ears.” Nobody understood. They were delicious. Professor Benthos tried holding one against his ear. To check.
textes.Monsieur Pression, notre voisin, l'a ins: Mr Pression, our neighbour, inspired it without meaning to: a gust of wind on the Edge Promenade, his umbrella blew inside out, and he yelled in B flat. A perfect B flat.
textes.Monsieur Prosper ! Elle a baissé ?: Monsieur Prosper! Has it gone down?
textes.Monsieur Prosper ! Vous estimez quoi, au: Mr Prosper! What are you valuing today?
textes.Monsieur Prosper a essayé de vendre ma t: Monsieur Prosper tried to sell my north tower to travellers. “Unbeatable view, absolute peace.” Aurore saw him to the door. Very peacefully. Absolutely.
textes.Monsieur Prosper a voulu vendre la tour: Mr Prosper tried to sell the castle's north tower to some travellers. He's been sending me flowers ever since I showed him out. The flowers are lovely. He's incorrigible.
textes.Monsieur Prosper m'a promis que je serai: Monsieur Prosper promised me I'd be the first to know if the price of the Cottage went down. That was twelve years ago. Every week, he lets me know it hasn't gone down. Very kind of him.
textes.Monsieur Prosper m'a vendu le vieux phar: Monsieur Prosper sold me the old lighthouse swearing it was a house. A hundred and forty steps, no furniture, draughts everywhere. It's the finest view of my life. I don't forgive him.
textes.Monsieur Prosper m'a vendu une maison «: Monsieur Prosper sold me a house “with a sea view”. It was the lighthouse. Empty, no furniture, with a hundred and forty steps. I live there anyway. The view really is lovely. But don't tell Prosper.
textes.Monsieur Prosper m'envoie des fleurs dep: Monsieur Prosper has been sending me flowers since I refused to sell the north tower. He hopes to change my mind. The flowers are lovely. My mind hasn't budged.
textes.Monsieur Prosper vend la Chaumière des G: Monsieur Prosper is selling Wisteria Cottage, in the Upper Town. Three hundred coins. He'll tell you it's a castle. It's a pretty house with a roof that leaks a bit. But the wisteria really is beautiful.
textes.Monsieur Prosper veut mon emplacement de: Mr Prosper wants my market spot for a “prestige boutique”. The best spot in Montjoie, next to the fountain! Three generations of Babette. Never.
textes.Monsieur Prosper, le marchand de maisons: Mr Prosper, the house seller of the Upper Town, is selling the Wisteria Cottage: a bed, a fireplace, a trophy shelf and a front covered in wisteria. Three hundred coins. He exaggerates everything. Except the wisteria.
textes.Monsieur Prosper. La tour nord n'est pas: Mr Prosper. The north tower is not for sale.
textes.Monsieur Prosper. Le phare n'est pas à v: Monsieur Prosper. The lighthouse is not for sale.
textes.Monsieur Radis ! Votre pommier va bien !: Mister Radis! Your apple tree is fine!
textes.Monsieur Radis m'a donné dix sur dix à m: Mister Radis gave my herbarium ten out of ten, and gave me the urge to climb everything. He talks to his tomatoes. I talk to trees. We're the same kind of family.
textes.Monsieur Rivet ! Ce matin, j'ai tapé sur: Mr Rivet! This morning I hit on the one!
textes.Monsieur Silas. Votre place près du feu: Mister Silas. Your seat by the fire is free.
textes.Monsieur Séverin me traite de gamin. J'a: Mr Séverin calls me a youngster. I'm seventy. He says I can complain when I'm his age. I'm practising. He tells everyone the story of the island rising. I've heard it a thousand times. I always listen to the end. He tells it well, the old rascal.
textes.Monsieur Tiburce n'était qu'un apprenti: Monsieur Tiburce was only an apprentice when I became his first customer. He polished my horns for an hour, trembling. I looked in the mirror and said: “Acceptable.” He burst into tears. I was concerned. It was explained to me that it was joy. I have never changed polisher.
textes.Monsieur Tiburce polit mes cornes chaque: Monsieur Tiburce has polished my horns every Monday for a hundred years. An excellent craftsman, a little too perfumed. I always tell him “acceptable”. Coming from me, that is a triumph.
textes.Monsieur Yvon a peur des grenouilles aut: Monsieur Yvon is as scared of frogs as I am, and he goes to the lake every day. He's a silent hero. I pray for him every morning. It doesn't work very well.
textes.Monsieur Yvon dit que la Duchesse avale: Monsieur Yvon says the Duchess swallows anything shiny. I'm shiny, when I zap.
textes.Monsieur Yvon est l'homme le plus courag: Mr Yvon is the bravest man on the island. He fishes here every day, trembling. I salute him!
textes.Monsieur Yvon, vous n'avez pas vu mon ch: Monsieur Yvon, have you seen my rosary?
textes.Monsieur Zigomar a lancé une fusée penda: Monsieur Zigomar launched a rocket during the ambassadors' dinner. It came in through the window and ended up in the soup. I served the soup anyway. Flambéed. I was congratulated.
textes.Monsieur Zigomar est un inventeur. C'est: Monsieur Zigomar is an inventor. That is to say, he blows things up and calls it progress. I banned him from the palace. He came back through the window. With a rocket.
textes.Monsieur Zigomar. Qu'avez-vous dans les: Monsieur Zigomar. What do you have in your hands?
textes.Monsieur Zénith. Vous sautez dans la cab: Mr Zénith. Are you jumping in the cabin?
textes.Monsieur désire un café ? Il est brûlant: Would sir like a coffee? It is scalding. I know, I tasted it with my finger.
textes.Monsieur et Madame Térieur ont deux fils: Mr. and Mrs. Side have two sons. What are their names?
textes.Monsieur le Baron ! Quel chapeau, aujour: My lord Baron! What a hat today!
textes.Monsieur le Baron, Bigorneau vous rend v: My lord Baron, Bigorneau is returning your hat.
textes.Monsieur le Baron, votre chapeau de la s: My lord Baron, your hat of the week.
textes.Monsieur le Baron, vous avez rendez-vous: My lord Baron, you have an appointment at ten.
textes.Monsieur le Baron, vous êtes tout décoif: Baron, your hair is all over the place!
textes.Monsieur le Ministre ! Où en est mon opé: Minister! How is my opera house coming along?
textes.Monsieur le maire est trop aimable. Si v: The mayor is too kind. If you're looking for a bed, our rooms are waiting for you. The night passes quickly here.
textes.Monsieur le maire, une holo-photo pour u: Mr. Mayor, a holo-photo for a tourist?
textes.Monsieur le maire. Vous avez fait vos vo: Mister Mayor. Done your vocal warm-ups?
Mister Thief. Tomorrow, I'll beat you.
textes.Monsieur Échec ne laisse pas gagner les: Mr Checkmate doesn't let children win. That's polite. I'd rather lose for real than win for pretend. Afterwards, I work out why.
textes.Mont Bolognaise — chemin de la Marmite\n:
Mount Bolognese — Cooking Pot path
Caution: unpredictable sauce eruptions.
Wear a bib.
textes.Mont Fumant. Il ronfle, il fume, il crac: Smoking Mountain. He snore, he smoke, he spit red. Never walk on red: red eat feet. Big-Beaks like fly above: hot air, they glide.
textes.Monte sur les passerelles, la vue est ma: Go up on the walkways, the view is magnificent. But don't look down.
textes.Monter ! Yes ! Tu as le cœur d'un liftie: Up! Yes! You've got the heart of a Cloud liftkeeper! We'll jump together on the next departure. Gently. Nova's watching us.
textes.Monter ? Comment ? Ah, MONTER ! Bon, bon: Up? What? Ah, UP! Fine, fine. Capucine will be pleased. But you'll come back down to see me, eh? Lifts work both ways.
textes.Monter au château du ciel et boire une b: To go up to the castle in the sky and share a fizz with the Sky Kings, as in my great-grandfather's day. A king talks better to a king. Especially over a fizz.
textes.Monter au sommet de la Flèche de Cristal: Fly to the top of the Crystal Spire (with the Star Glider) and give the Heart back its shards and its light
textes.Monter au sommet de la Tour Penchée en l: Levitate up to the top of the Leaning Tower (key 8 then V; in VR, left trigger) and ring the bell (E)
textes.Monter au sommet du Mont Fusain: Climb to the summit of Mount Charcoal
textes.Monter au sommet du Mont Fusain (le chem: Climb to the summit of Mount Charcoal (the path starts at the north exit of the clearing) and take the pot of purple at the foot of the cairn
textes.Monter dans le Village des Arbres-Maison: Climb up into the Treehouse Village
textes.Monter en haut de la Cascade d'Encre (pa: Climb to the top of the Ink Waterfall (by the Mount Charcoal path, then along the stream) and take the pot of orange by the water, on the Lip
textes.Monter jusqu'à la Cité des Nuées avec to: To go up to the City of Clouds with my whole class and Miss Nautile, meet Lili at the edge of her island, and give her the singing shell. She'll give me a kite. We'll fly it together, above the sea. And if it rains that day, it'll be perfect. I won't open an umbrella. I haven't got one anyway.
textes.Monter jusqu'à la Marmite, en haut du Mo: Climb up to the Cooking Pot, at the top of Mount Bolognese
textes.Monter sur Astralys par le rayon d'accue: Go up to Astralys on the welcome beam (the glowing buoy, in the north-west of the archipelago)
textes.Monter sur la scène de la Halle Hurlante: To get up on the stage of the Howling Hall. Just once. With real drumsticks. Play with the Bilge Rats, close my eyes, and when I open them again, see everyone jumping. Even Dad. A little.
textes.Monter sur le Grand Spaghetti Volant et: To ride on the Great Flying Spaghetti and fly around the archipelago hanging from a noodle. And throw meatballs at the seagulls. And be back in time for snack.
textes.Monter un jour dans le Funiculaire avec: To ride the Funicular one day with my blank notebook, cross the four worlds, and write everything down myself, for once: the Strata, Hautefond, the Clouds. Then come back down, climb onto a bench on Pearl Square and read it all out loud. The greatest newspaper at the bottom of the sea. Written by the bottom of the sea.
