textes.À moitié, Coyotl ! Tlaco a bu l'autre mo: Half, Coyotl! Tlaco drank the other half!
textes.À moitié. Il y a un plancher, un pilote,: Half. There's a floor, a pilot, windows and coffee. Achille has none of that. Not even a roof. Especially not a roof.
textes.À mon arrivée, le Couvercle n'avait pas: When I arrived, the Lid had no guard. One Sunday, someone struck it three times, for fun. The Cooking Pot spat all afternoon. The Borgo was red from the ground to the rooftops. The next day I said to the Reverend: “You need a guard.” He said: “We need a guard.” We agreed right away.
textes.À mon premier Conseil, j'avais vingt-hui: At my first Council, I was twenty-eight and had a file on gutters. Mr Pascal spoke against it for forty minutes. Then he voted for it. On the way out, he told me: “I wanted to see if you could hold your ground.” I held my ground. We've been friends ever since. Well, he says we're not.
textes.À mon premier combat dans l'Arène, j'ava: At my first fight in the Arena, I was so scared that I closed my eyes. I walked straight ahead, slowly, and my opponent stepped out of the arena all by himself, backwards, so as not to get squashed. The crowd roared. I opened my eyes and said: “Sorry.” Since then, I always say sorry. It brings good luck.
textes.À mon retour, un slime est tombé dans mo: When I came back, a slime fell into my cauldron. I tried to get it out, spilled honey on it, and the mixture healed a cut I had on my finger. Slime jelly! A marvellous ingredient. Since then I buy it from adventurers. They think I'm joking. They look at me oddly. I heal them anyway.
textes.À mon tout premier concert, j'avais si p: At my very first gig, I was so scared I barely played. Nobody could hear me. Larsen secretly turned up my bass, very gradually. I only found out a year later. He said: “PEOPLE NEEDED TO HEAR YOU.” He shouted it, obviously.
textes.À mon âge, chaque matin est un cadeau. M: At my age, every morning is a gift. Even rainy mornings. Especially rainy mornings: nobody asks me to work.
At my age, every knot is a victory.
textes.À mon âge, je mange lentement. Ça me lai: At my age, I eat slowly. It gives me time to take a second plate.
At my age, there's plenty of time.
textes.À mon âge, on ne souffle plus, mon grand: At my age, sweetheart, you don't blow anymore. You wait.
textes.À mon âge, une chouquette par jour. Le d: At my age, one sugar puff a day. The doctor said “one”. He didn't say “a small one”.
textes.À neuf ans, je suis allé voir l'Amirale: When I was nine, I went to see the Admiral to become a cabin boy. She said: “Ring the bell on time for a month, without a mistake.” I got it wrong four times. She took me on anyway. She said the four times were to check whether Carène was listening. She's kind, the Admiral. But secretly.
textes.À neuf ans, on m'a envoyé à la Maison de: At nine, I was sent to the House of Life. The master made me copy out the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor: a sailor is stranded on an island, and a giant serpent, covered in gold, talks to him very kindly. Three hundred times I copied it. I dreamed of chatty serpents. Even today, I recite it with my eyes closed. It puts the pupils to sleep. That's useful.
textes.À notre première répétition dans la cale: At our first rehearsal in the hold, the rats came to listen. I asked if we should keep the name Bilge Rats. Clou thought for a long time, then said his first full sentence in front of me: “We keep the name.” I nearly cried. It was the longest speech of the year.
textes.À onze ans, ma première Grande Course. J: At eleven, my first Great Race. I shoot off like an arrow… and at the root bend, just before the Lookout, I fall. Twisted ankle. Pépin, who'd fallen too, carried me on his back to the finish. We came last, together. Last! Me! Since then, I've never finished behind anyone again. Hop.
textes.À personne ? Oh, mais il faut ! Ce n'est: To nobody? Oh, but you must! It's not forbidden to give some to yourself, you know. Here, next time, I'll give you one. You'll be your own first customer.
textes.À personne, et c'est bien ça le souci !: To no one, and that's the problem! It's Brioche. Ginger and white, like a golden brioche, see? Every morning at six, she comes down from the roof, takes ONE sardine from me, just one, very politely, and goes back up to eat it while watching me. She doesn't steal, she helps herself. She's dignified, that cat. More dignified than the mayor. But there it is: she has nobody. In winter, she sleeps against the harbour master's chimney, and Odette pretends not to see her. I can't take her, I have three floors and an allergic husband. You travel… A cat that travels, I think she'd like that. But she won't let anyone near her. Except… Pauline, the Grand Hotel's chambermaid, knits on the terrace: one day, Brioche came to play with her ball of yarn. She even purred. Go see Pauline!
textes.À pleine vapeur ! J'ai réparé onze chose: Full steam ahead! I fixed eleven things today: a toaster, a guitar, two skateboards, a boiler, an umbrella and the same lamp five times. That lamp has a problem. Or it likes me.
textes.À pleine vapeur ! J'ai trouvé le bleu !: Full steam ahead! I've found the blue! The real blue of the crystals in the mine: Opaline, from the Workshop of Lights, gave me some crushed crystal powder. On the rock, it glows in the dark. Tonight, the Wall will light up. Come and see.
textes.À pleine vapeur ! La Ligne a rouvert, {s: Full steam ahead! The Line has reopened, {surnom}! Last night there were people from up top in the pit. In hats! One gentleman jumped up and down with his hat on for the whole song. He didn't lose it. Respect.
textes.À pleine vapeur ! Le rail numéro sept es: Full steam ahead! Rail number seven is straightened, my guitar is tuned, and Ysaé came down to eat with us at lunchtime. Three bits of good news before one o'clock. I'm going to make a song of it.
textes.À pleine vapeur ! Quarante-deux bols ser: Full steam ahead! Forty-two bowls served at lunch. Eleven of them to folk from up top. A gentleman with a moustache asked me for the menu. I told him: “I'm the menu.” He had what I gave him. He came back for seconds twice.
textes.À pleins poumons !: At the top of my lungs!
textes.À plus ! Attention en sortant, la porte: See you! Careful on the way out, the door has a spring. And it's not my son. Well, not this time.
textes.À plus ! Ce soir, les Soupapes jouent à: See you! Tonight the Valves play at eight. It's pay what you can: you pay in applause.
textes.À plus ! Et si tu croises ma fille en ha: See you! And if you run into my daughter up top, tell her her dad still plays too loud. It'll reassure her.
textes.À plus ! Et si tu vois Maîtresse Capucin: See you! And if you see Mistress Capucine, tell her I looked down today. Once. A little.
textes.À plus ! Fais attention sur le Pont. Pas: See you! Careful on the Bridge. Not because of the Chasm: because of Ressort, who crosses it on his skateboard.
textes.À plus ! Faut que j'y retourne : Maîtres: See you! I've got to get back: Mistress Brunehaut counts the taps. She knows when I miss one.
textes.À plus ! Je retourne au Skatepark. La Ba: See you! I'm going back to the Skatepark. The Whale's waiting for me!
textes.À plus ! Le Petit Plongeon m'attend. Il: See you! The Little Diver's waiting for me. He's going “bloop” with impatience.
textes.À plus ! Moi, je redescends. Puis je rem: See ya! Me, I'm going back down. Then up again. Then down again. That's the job!
textes.À plus ! Moi, je remonte. Puis je redesc: See you! I'm heading back up. Then back down. Then back up. A hundred and forty metres of happiness, there and back!
textes.À plus ! Passe à la Halle ce soir : c'es: See ya! Come by the Hall tonight: it's free, it's loud, and it's full of love. Mostly loud.
textes.À plus ! Quand tu reviendras, regarde le: See you! When you come back, look at the Wall. You might be a little taller on it.
textes.À plus ! Tu as des choses dans tes poche: See you! Got things in your pockets? Keep them. They might be treasures.
textes.À plus tard ! Attention aux traits d'enc: See you later! Watch out for the ink lines, they're slippery after rain.
textes.À plus tard ! Et ne cours pas sur le Pon: See you later! And don't run on the Bridge after a meal, it sloshes the stew about.
textes.À plus tard ! Et ne te penche pas trop à: See you later! And don't lean too far over the railing: the Floor is a long way down, and it never gives hats back.
textes.À plus tard ! Et si tout le monde se tai: See you later! And if everyone around you suddenly goes quiet, go quiet too: it's the Great Singer passing over the Dome.
textes.À plus tard ! Prochain départ dans vingt: See you later! Next departure in twenty minutes. Or twenty minutes and four seconds. Don't tell Gaspard.
textes.À plus tard ! Si tu croises un navet qui: See you later! If you meet a running turnip, don't tell it where I live.
textes.À plus tard ! Si tu entends siffler, ce: See you later! If you hear whistling, it's not a train: it's Firmin's hot chocolate, ready to go.
textes.À plus tard ! Si tu entends un grand « B: See you later! If you hear a big “BONG”, don't worry: it's the Great Clock. Or Mistress Brunehaut laughing.
textes.À plus tard, {surnom} ! Et essuie-toi la: See you later, {surnom}! And wipe your lip: you've got a chocolate moustache. Welcome to the club!
textes.À plus tard, {surnom} ! Reviens pour la: See you later, {surnom}! Come back for the Great Table: there'll be plenty for everyone.
textes.À plus tard. Je retourne à mes vitres. E: See you later. Back to my panes. They're waiting for me. They don't say so, but I know.
textes.À plus, {surnom} ! Et si tu entends deux: See you, {surnom}! And if you hear two knocks, then one, answer! It means hello, thank you.
textes.À plus, {surnom} ! Et tiens bon le manch: See you, {surnom}! And keep a firm grip on the handle, in life as at the forge!
textes.À plus. La ligne a rouvert : un de ces s: See you. The line has reopened: one of these evenings, I'll take you down. Promise. Get your ears ready.
textes.À plus. Quand la ligne rouvrira, je t'em: Later. When the line reopens, I'll take you down below. Promise. Get your ears ready.
textes.À plus. Si tu entends un larsen, ce n'es: Later. If you hear feedback, it's not us. Well, it is. But it's on purpose.
textes.À quarante ans, Gunnar m'a parié une cho: When I was forty, Gunnar bet me a mug that I wouldn't go all the way to the edge of the crater. I went. Alone. I came back with a shard of obsidian and singed eyebrows. My uncle shouted for an hour, then he named me scout of the slopes. Gunnar still owes me that mug.
textes.À quarante ans, Lyra a voulu regarder pa: At forty, Lyra wanted to look over the mist, and she fell off the highest walkway. Ankle on backwards. I bandaged it with sage leaves and made her drink my potion. She pulled such a face that in the Bois-Doré they still say “to pull a Lyra face”. I take it as a compliment.
textes.À quarante ans, elle est montée au bord: At forty, she climbed to the rim of the crater on a dare. Alone. She came back down with a shard of obsidian and singed eyebrows. I shouted for an hour. Then I made her a scout. Now she shouts less than me. She learnt.
textes.À quarante ans, j'ai trouvé un petit cor: At forty, I found a little crow that had fallen in the ash, all lopsided, squawking louder than himself. I fed him cheese. He never left. He's the one who taught me to talk to crows. Well, to listen to them. That's Croâ. He says he's an eagle. He isn't.
textes.À quarante ans, j'avais tout et je m'enn: At forty, I had everything and I was bored. One morning, I put a vase out on the pavement with a sign: “Help yourself.” A child took it for his mum. The next day, I put out a chair. Then everything else. In a month, I had nothing left. And fifty friends.
textes.À quatorze ans, j'ai construit ma premiè: At fourteen, I built my first boat, all by myself, out of papyrus. I called her The Dragonfly. She floated to the middle of the river, very proud, then came apart like a badly plaited braid. I swam home pushing my basket of fish in front of me. My father said: “You swim well. Like your great-grandfather.”
textes.À quatorze ans, j'ai fabriqué une basse: At fourteen, I made a bass out of a broomstick and three rubber bands. It went “bzoing”. I played it on the quay all day long. One day, a girl with a red mohawk stopped and said: “You, you've got rhythm.” It was Rouille. The next day, I was in the band.
textes.À quatorze ans, je suis allée frapper ch: At fourteen, I went and knocked on Professor Boum's door. He said: “Stand there. No, there. Further back.” I stayed six years. Four roofs. I swept up soot and dreamed of colours. He taught me to listen to a boiler: when it sings, all's well; when it goes quiet, you run. It's the best lesson of my life.
textes.À quatorze ans, je suis montée à l'Acadé: At fourteen, I went up to the Academy. The healing mistress was old Bourrache, who smelled of camphor and scolded plants that grew crooked. She taught me that you don't heal with your hands, but with your ears: you must listen before you touch. It took me ten years to understand. I'm not sure I've finished.
textes.À quatorze ans, un cirque est passé en v: At fourteen, a circus came to town: the Two Moons Circus. I saw a clown fall twelve times in a row, and everyone laughed, even my father, for one second. That very night I packed my bag. I carried buckets, fed the goats, and learned to juggle with potatoes. The goats ate the balls.
textes.À quatre ans, j'ai démonté la montre de: At four, I took my grandfather's watch apart. I put it back together at four and a half. There was one part left over. The watch worked anyway. I kept the part in a little box. Forty years later, I still don't know where it goes. I look at it every evening. It looks back at me.
textes.À quinfe ans, f'ai embarqué fur un brick: At fifteen, I thigned on to a brig called the Theagull. I thcrubbed the deck, mended the netth, learned the knotth. Much later, Gontran bought her and renamed her the Thcarlet Widow. Me, I changed captainth, not thipth. Back then, nobody called me Thans-Dents. They called me Thébathtien. Ah, it wath a fine name, Thébathtien.
textes.À quinze ans, Tréphine m'a donné son car: At fifteen, Tréphine gave me her green journal, all warped with seawater. Three hundred recipes, half of them crossed out. “The crossings-out are what I learned,” she used to say. I set up the infirmary on the lower deck, between the hammocks: the patients are already lying down, it saves time.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai cousu un soufflet pou: At fifteen, I sewed a bellows for Jos's forge, my first job all on my own. The stitches were crooked. I've offered a hundred times to redo it. He always refuses: he says it blows better crooked. I mostly think he doesn't want to hurt my feelings. With Jos, you never know.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai embarqué avec Corenti: At fifteen, I went out with Corentin, who was a fisherman before he was a talker. He taught me to gut a mackerel in three moves, and then to say it weighed three pounds. The three moves, I forgot. The three pounds, never. That's how you become a real Carène fisherman.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai fait le tour de toute: At fifteen, I went round every pane of the dome with an old mechanic. He taught me to tap them: “ting” means healthy; “tonk” means tired. At number one hundred and four, I saw a little bubble trapped in the glass. He told me: “It's been there since the first day. It's holding. Like us.” It's my favourite pane.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai frappé à la cabane de: At fifteen, I knocked on Barnabé's hut. I wanted to know how he'd built it all by himself, after his shipwreck. He taught me sailors' knots, how to read the wind before putting up a roof, and that planks have a grain, like maps have a direction. He talked to Gaston the whole lesson. Gaston already knew everything.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai posé mon chapeau sur: At fifteen, I put my hat down on the Great Square and played. A single coin fell in. It was Grandpa Ébène's. He said: “Come and play behind my stories.” Since then, I play for him: low notes for the dragons, soft ones for the princesses, and a very long one when he forgets what comes next.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai pris la corde. Père a: At fifteen, I took the rope. Father said: “Are you sure?” I said: “Hrmm.” With me, it goes up in silence. The passengers came back. I know the story of every wicker changed. And every rope. Four wickers. Six ropes. One basket. Grandpa's.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai trouvé une table de m: At fifteen, I found a broken mixing desk in a skip. A hundred and twelve knobs. It took me a year to work out what the first three did. The other hundred and nine, I still don't know. But they look very serious. People think I use them all.
textes.À quinze ans, j'ai voulu inventer un car: At fifteen, I wanted to invent a fizzing caramel. It fizzed. Then it whistled. Then it took out the kitchen window and a good part of the ceiling. My mother, covered in sugar, looked at me for a long time, and advised me to charge for my explosions in future. Ten years later, I opened L'Alambic in her sweet shop. The shelves still smell of caramel.
textes.À quinze ans, j'étais apprenti chez le v: At fifteen, I was apprenticed to the old polisher of the Upper Town. My first real client was Asmodin, the palace butler. He watched me work for an hour, without a word. Then he looked at himself in the mirror and said: “Acceptable.” I wept with joy. He still comes, every Monday. He still says “acceptable”.
textes.À quinze ans, j'étais mousse. On est arr: At fifteen I was a cabin girl. We arrived here, Sel disguised as a salt merchant. The harbour women sold us sacks of sand. Sand! And a girl of twenty, Fatima, saw me skinny as a herring and gave me a bowl of harira. That night, I was the one carrying the lantern when Sel hid his chest in the caves. Where? Ha! Drink up.
textes.À quinze ans, j'étais pêcheur, et longte: At fifteen, I was a fisherman, and for a long time I kept my boat alongside Driss's. At thirty-five, my father died, and the port gave me his staff. The first morning, I set the price of sardines. The whole port shouted: too high, too low, too early. I held firm. The next day, they shouted less. That's what being amin is: you listen to the shouting, then you decide.
textes.À quinze ans, je comptais les pièces plu: At fifteen, I counted coins faster than the eye could see them. A captain accused me of cheating in front of the whole room. My father put a coin on the table, hid it under three cups, and said: “Find it.” The captain lost ten times in a row. He left grumbling that I had silver fingers. The name stuck. The captain didn't.
textes.À quinze ans, je gardais le petit Clotai: At fifteen, I used to mind little Clotaire, the neighbours' son, who fell asleep everywhere. I'd wake him with a nudge of my elbow every time he nodded off over his homework. He learnt to read thanks to my elbows. When he joined the temple, I walked him all the way to the door so he wouldn't run off. He still rubs his ribs when he sees me.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis descendu au port a: At fifteen, I went down to the port with a bundle and a hammer. I learned iron from a blacksmith, wood from a carpenter, and money on my own. I'm the one who laid the keel of the Stubborn Seagull. Three years in the shipyard. On the day she sailed, the shipowner told me: “You built her, you fix her.” I came aboard. I shouldn't have.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis entré dans la mari: At fifteen, I joined the king's navy, lookout on the Faithful, a brand-new galleon. I had a copper spyglass and a uniform that was too big. For two years, I saw whales, islands, storms, and once a sea serpent. Nobody believed me. Nor did the serpent, I think: it left straight away.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis entrée en apprenti: At fifteen, I was apprenticed to old Mr Taquet, the Strata mechanic. He fixed everything: clocks, pumps, locomotives. He used to say: “Nothing gets thrown away. A lonely screw is a screw waiting for its friends.” When he retired, he gave me his toolbox. His very last sale was an old locomotive chocolate machine, to a certain Firmin, from up top. I'd patched it up the day before. The whistle's my doing.
textes.À quinze ans, je suis entrée à la Fabriq: At fifteen I joined the Works, apprenticed to Master Rivet. He didn't talk, he showed. And while welding he hummed an old shepherds' song, always out of tune, always the same one. It was with him that I made the Zéphyr: me the plans and the gas, him the giant sewing machine for the envelope. We were a very good machine, the two of us.
textes.À quinze ans, l'ancien crieur, le vieux: When I was fifteen, the old crier, old Bastien, lost his voice shouting the results of the turnip contest. He handed his post over to me. Brunehaut cast me a bell. It weighs eleven kilos. I named it Marguerite, after my grandmother, because they're both very loud and very tender. Well, my grandmother was tender.
textes.À quinze ans, ma mère m'a laissé son tou: At fifteen, my mother left me her wheel. My first bowls all leaned the same way, as if they were listening to something. Then one day, they stood up straight. My first big tagine dish, I made it for my aunt Zineb, at the Fondouk. It's still there. She shows it to every caravan driver, and adds that I'm ready to marry. Thanks, khalti.
textes.À quinze ans, ma première traversée. Tro: At fifteen, my first crossing. Three days of sand, all the way to Tazira. On the last morning we crossed the last dune, and there was the sea. All blue, to the end of the world. The others talked, laughed, ran to the water. I sat down. I said nothing for an hour. My father said: “Good. He understood.”
textes.À quinze ans, mon oncle Pech, le vieil a: At fifteen, my uncle Pech, the old astronomer, took me into the observatory. He taught me Venus: she rises in the morning, disappears, rises in the evening, disappears, and comes back every five hundred and eighty-four days. I copied his tables into a folded bark book. It's there, in my niche. It smells of smoke, rain and old age. So do I.
textes.À quinze ans, mon père voulait que je so: At fifteen, my father wanted me to be a miller. The mill was too noisy for me to sleep. The temple, though, was silent. Philomène walked me to the door to make sure I wouldn't run off. The old priest looked at me and said: “You look well rested. You'll make a good priest.”
textes.À quinze ans, on m'a confié le huehuetl: At fifteen, I was given the huehuetl in the square: a hollow trunk as tall as me, with a skin stretched over it. The first evening, I played so long I couldn't feel my hands. The dancers stayed until dawn. The next day, my hands were blue. Like the hips of the ball players of Yaxché.
textes.À quinze ans, un soir, j'ai entendu un b: At fifteen, one evening, I heard a terrible racket on the other side of the Chasm. My parents said it was “the Frondeurs”. I crossed the Bridge for the first time. I was so scared I sang all the way across, to give myself courage. When I got to the other side, a boy was banging on a boiler. He was a beat behind.
textes.À quinze heures précises. Et sans triche: At three o'clock sharp. And no cheating.
textes.À réparer ? Bien. Le monde a besoin de g: Mend them? Good. The world needs people like you. And glue. If one day you have a cracked pot, bring it along: I'll show you how to stitch clay back together.
textes.À sa première leçon, la petite Sulfura a: In her first lesson, little Sulfura set my beard alight with a snap of her fingers. The whole class froze. I said: “Excellent! Now, put it out.” It took her three minutes, crying and laughing at the same time. I gave her the best mark of the year. As for my beard, it never grew back as long.
textes.À sa première nuit, elle avait seize ans: On her first night she was sixteen, with trembling knees. Just as she was lifting the moon out of the pond, she stumbled, and the whole Circle held its breath. I whispered to her from my moss: “You don't lift it, little one. You rock it.” She rocked. Since then, she's the one.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai fabriqué ma première p: At sixteen, I made my first sap potion, with herbs from my mother's garden. I tasted it myself, on principle. My eyes turned green. They stayed that way, and they glow a little in the dark. It's very handy for reading labels at night. I've never regretted it.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai fait mon propre ras-el: At sixteen, I made my own ras el hanout. Thirty-two spices, weighed to the grain. And a thirty-third ingredient that nobody knows. My mother smelled it, smiled, and said nothing. The caravan men bought three sacks and took it all the way to Carène. My blend saw Carène before I did. It travels better than me: it doesn't complain.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai lu une annonce de Lumi: At sixteen, I read an advert from Lumina: “Seeking someone who isn't afraid of the night.” I went to see her. I only said three words: “I like night.” She gave me a pole and the list of street lamps. Since then, I've lit up the city every evening. I've given every lamp a name. Gustave flickers when he's happy.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai poussé la porte du Pai: At sixteen, I pushed open the door of the Pain Doré to buy a baguette. I made a big gesture while talking and knocked over a whole basket of croissants. Margaux looked at me and said: “You've got energy, you. Can you knead?” The next day, at four in the morning, there I was, in an apron.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai pris la pierre de ma g: At sixteen, I took my grandmother's stone and went down alone. I brought back pearly shells, sea urchins, once an old silver spoon. Now I dive for Momo's necklaces, for curious folk, for me. Underwater, there's no time. That's why I lose track of it up here too.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai quitté la confiserie a: At sixteen, I left the sweet shop with a box of humbugs and three bone dice. On the harbour, some sailors were playing on a barrel. I sat down. By morning, I had their coins, their caps and a place on their boat. Since then, I've never had a real job. Dice, my friend, are better than a job: they're a conversation with luck.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai suivi une caravane jus: At sixteen, I followed a caravan all the way to the oasis, my sardine tin on my back. There, an old musician listened to me and laughed. Then he made me a real guembri: a wooden neck, a stretched camel skin, three strings. He told me: “Inside, you must put the desert night.” It took me two years to understand.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai trouvé une bombe de pe: At sixteen, I found a can of green spray paint in a skip. I painted a tree on a grey wall in my neighbourhood. The next day, someone had hung a swing on the tree. A real one, on the wall. I understood that walls could answer back. I came to Boucan to hear them.
textes.À seize ans, j'ai vu le ciel faire une c: At sixteen, I saw the sky turn a colour nobody had ever seen. For three seconds. Between pink and green, with a touch of gold. I had a brush behind my ear. I painted it. The canvas hangs at the Council. The First Councillor says the colour is called “Ombeline”. Since then, I never take my brush off.
textes.À seize ans, j'avais mon numéro : la Rou: At sixteen, I had my own act: the Redhead and Her Blades. Marcel, my partner, stood on a big spinning wheel, and I planted the knives all around him, a finger's width away. One evening, in front of three hundred people, with the wheel spinning, he asked me for a raise. I raised a knife, thought about it, and put it down. I changed careers that very night.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré aux Rails des: At sixteen, I joined the Strata Railways as an apprentice. On the first day, the old foreman gave me a spanner and said: “Listen to the rail before you tighten it.” I tapped it. It sang. I realised I'd found a job where you could make music without anyone complaining.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré en apprentiss: At sixteen, I was apprenticed to Honoré Cogne, the greatest automaton maker in Cliquetis. Thirty years in the workshop. As my old master used to say: “A gear never lies. It's the clockmaker who lies.” He started the chess-playing automaton, then he died, twenty-two years ago, without finishing it. The workshop and the automaton were left to me. The golden gear, to his grandson.

At sixteen, I was apprenticed to an old clockmaker on the Grand Square. Forty-two years later, I still have fine oil under my fingernails. For thirty years, I've kept and wound the great clock of the Academy, every morning at seven. I sleep with three alarm clocks. They ring at the same second. If one of them lags, I don't sleep for a week.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré à l'école de: At sixteen, I joined the Guard school. I was the tallest, the most serious, and the clumsiest with a sword. My instructor said I fought like a drawbridge: slowly, but nobody gets past. I took it as a compliment. I still take it that way.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entré à la Fabrique: At sixteen, I joined the Works as Master Rivet's apprentice. Sweepers, carriers, arms, wheels. Master Rivet doesn't say much. He shows you. He puts a part in front of you, says “Hm”, and you understand. Or you start again. I started again a lot. In the end, I understood.
textes.À seize ans, je suis entrée chez la viei: At sixteen, I went to work for old Madame Carillon, who made music boxes on Springs Street. She taught me cylinders and pins: one pin, one note; one crooked pin, a wrong note forever. When she passed away, she left me her tools, with a little note: “Plant straight.”
textes.À seize ans, la Guilde cherchait quelqu': At sixteen, the Guild was looking for someone to tidy a drawer. Just one. It held forty years of papers, two sandwiches turned to stone, a troll's glove and a love letter from Master Hugues that was never sent. I sorted everything in a week. The letter, I filed under “Confidential”. He doesn't know I read it.
textes.À seize ans, les genoux de maman n'ont p: At sixteen, Mum's knees gave out. I danced alone for the first time. Oh… I was so scared. When it came to lifting the moon out of the pond, I stumbled. Mother Moon whispered to me: “You don't lift it, you rock it.” Since then, I'm the dancer. Mum lives in peace with the does of the deep forest. I visit her every season.
textes.À seize ans, ma mère m'a offert un métie: At sixteen, my mother gave me a loom, an old one that creaked like an inn door. I spent a whole winter at it. Silk, cotton, northern wool, and the desert dyes. The first cloth, I laid against my mother's cheek. She closed her eyes and said: “Soft as a cloud.” I've said it to all my customers ever since. It's hers.
textes.À seize ans, un caboteur s'est arrêté su: At sixteen, a coaster stopped at our island for fresh water. Its helmsman had a fever, and nobody knew how to steer. I raised my hand: I'd learned on my father's boat. I brought the coaster to the next port without a scratch. The skipper kept me on. The crew called me Winkle. I protested. It lasted six years.
textes.À seize ans, une vieille tatoueuse est p: At sixteen, an old tattooist came by the shipyard. She had anchors on her arms, fish on her hands and a little dragon behind her ear. I followed her for three years, from port to port, preparing her inks. She used to say: “Skin isn't canvas. It breathes, it moves, it remembers.” When she left for good, she left me her needles.
textes.À sept ans, en haut, à Hautefond, j'ai t: When I was seven, up in Hautefond, I found a little blue pebble that glowed in the dark in one of my grandfather's boxes. “It comes from down below,” he told me. I kept it under my pillow for years. I read every book about crystals. One was missing: the one that explained why it glowed. I decided to write it.
textes.À sept ans, j'ai construit une cabane en: At seven, I built a cardboard hut in my grandmother's garden, and sold it to my sister for her marbles. “Garden view, watertight roof, quiet neighbourhood.” The next day, it rained, and the hut blew away. My sister demanded her marbles back. I told her: “The plot, however, is still there.”
textes.À sept ans, j'ai démonté le grille-pain: At seven, I took my mother's toaster apart. I never put it back together. She bought me a toolbox for my eighth birthday, saying: “Now you fix things.” The toaster still works. It's in my workshop. It makes heart-shaped toast. It's a bug. I kept it.
textes.À sept ans, j'ai inventé la cuillère. J': At seven, I invented the spoon. I'd drawn it all: a handle, a little hollow at the end… My grandmother handed me a spoon. Without a word. At nine, I invented the kite. At ten, the sock. I've always had my ideas… just after everyone else. My grandmother said I was one idea behind. Just one. That's not much, one idea.
textes.À sept ans, j'ai voulu compter les étoil: When I was seven, I wanted to count the stars before going to sleep. At three hundred, my mother closed the curtains. I kept counting in my head. At a thousand, she bought thicker curtains. At two thousand, I bought a telescope with my savings. She gave up on curtains.
textes.À sept ans, j'ai vu Agrafe imprimer le B: When I was seven, I saw Agrafe printing the Boucanier. I said: “Me too.” He laughed. So I made my own fanzine: “The Cherry on the Zine”. Drawings, interviews, and the column “Tornade's Blunders”. Agrafe prints it for me. The last issue sold better than his. He says it's the horses.
textes.À sept ans, je suis entrée au temple. Am: At seven, I entered the temple. Amenemhat, who still had hair back then, taught me the signs. He had me copy out the morning hymn, again and again. One day, I drew a little sleeping cat in the margin, to rest. He said nothing. He kept the papyrus. He still shows it to visitors, thirty-eight years later.
textes.À sept ans, je suis tombé du grand chêne: When I was seven, I fell out of the big oak in the Mist Park. Three branches, one lawn, and not a scratch. As I got up, I shouted “Again!”. My mother shouted something else. That very evening, she took me to see the Line's capsule. She said: “If you want to go up, go up with a cable.”
textes.À sept ans, mon grand-père m'a emmenée d: When I was seven, my grandfather took me into the cave, under the great ridge. He showed me the round stone, carved all over. I took out my little screwdriver to take it apart. I couldn't. It's the only thing in the world I've never managed to take apart. It was warm, {surnom}. Like a hand. I still dream about it. The last time I went up, black brambles were blocking the cave.
textes.À sept heures zéro une, j'ai déréglé l'h: At seven-oh-one, I messed up Tempo's fountain clock. At seven-oh-two, he grabbed me by the collar. At seven-oh-three, he forgave me. I told him: “See, even your anger is on time.” He made a funny face. I think he was trying not to laugh.
textes.À sept heures zéro zéro, j'ai réglé l'ho: At seven-oh-oh, I set the fountain clock. At seven-oh-one, Quark had put it out of order. At seven-oh-two, I grabbed him by the collar. At seven-oh-three, I'd forgiven him. He told me: “See, even your anger is on time.” The little one is right.
textes.À sept heures. Ne sois pas en retard. Co: Seven o'clock. Don't be late. Like yesterday.
textes.À six ans, j'ai dessiné un dragon sur le: At six, I drew a dragon on my bedroom wall. My parents covered it with wallpaper. I drew it again on the wallpaper, bigger. They did it again. So did I. After four layers, they gave up. The dragon's still there, under four layers of wallpaper. He's nice and warm.
textes.À six ans, j'ai démonté la radio de ma m: At six, I took my mother's radio apart. Completely. There were a hundred and twelve pieces. I didn't know how to put it back together. My mother cried a bit. Brasero came by, looked at the pieces spread out on the table, and said: “Taking apart is half the way. The other half, we'll do together.” We put it back together. There were three pieces left over. It worked better.
textes.À six ans, j'ai fait mon premier grand c: At six, I made my first big hip shot. The ball flew over the wall and landed on the head of Ah Kin Pech, who was watching Venus. It bounced and landed back on mine! Two identical bumps. Everyone says he's the one who saw stars. I saw them too. But I don't admit it.
textes.À six ans, j'ai planté un fraisier sur l: When I was six, I planted a strawberry plant on my windowsill. It gave a single strawberry, a tiny one. I cut it in four, for my parents, my brother and me. It was the best strawberry in the world. Today, one of my strawberries feeds four families. But none has ever tasted as good.
textes.À six ans, j'avais un ballon rouge, un b: When I was six, I had a red balloon, a party balloon. I let go of it by accident. It went up, and up, until I couldn't see it any more. I cried, then I decided I'd go and fetch it. That's why the Albatross is red. So it'll recognise me, if it's still out there somewhere.
textes.À six ans, ma mère m'a fait monter dans: When I was six, my mother took me up in the cabin. I was so frightened I held the rail with both hands and my teeth. She told me: “Look at the people, not the drop.” I looked at the people. They were smiling. I was never afraid again. Well, almost.
textes.À six ans, mon grand-père m'a fait asseo: When I was six, my grandfather sat me on the Funicular's control desk. “Don't touch anything, look outside.” The cabin came out of the cliff, and the whole city lit up beneath us, in the blue. I forgot to breathe. My grandfather patted me on the back: “Breathe, lad. Down here, air is free, but you have to take it.” I've been breathing ever since. And driving.
textes.À six heures ? C'était tout doux, à six: At six? It was ever so gentle, at six!
textes.À soixante ans, j'ai suivi une chèvre ég: At sixty, I followed a stray goat all the way to the fumaroles. In the hot ash, there were little red glimmers. I bit into one. I sneezed a flame, I cried, I laughed, and I knew I had my stew. The white ones, I tasted those too. A week of being a dragon. Never again.
textes.À son arrivée, il a exigé une chambre «: When he arrived, he demanded a room “facing south-west, towards Atlantis”. I got out the hotel plan and a compass. Only one room faced south-west, give or take two degrees. He asked whether the bed could be turned two degrees. I turned the bed two degrees. The house is at the service of science.
textes.À son premier combat, il a fermé les yeu: At his first fight, he closed his eyes and walked straight ahead, very slowly. His opponent backed out of the arena so as not to get flattened. The crowd went wild. Gorgoth opened his eyes and said: “Sorry.” Ever since, before every fight, I shout: “AND HE'S GOING TO SAY SORRY!” The crowd loves it.
textes.À son premier concert, Mouette jouait si: At her first concert, Mouette played so softly nobody could hear her. She was scared. I turned her up in secret, notch by notch, all through the concert. By the end, she was smiling. I only told her a year later. She did the seagull cry right in my ear. It took me three days to recover.
textes.À tes souhaits, Kraxx. C'est du poivre d: Bless you, Kraxx. It's ash pepper today.
textes.À toi ! Moi, je fais la tour de contrôle: Your turn! I'll be the control tower!
textes.À toi. Tu l'as creusée il y a deux cents: Yours. You dug it two hundred years ago.
textes.À tous mes clients, je fais la pub du dé: I advertise Kevin's challenge to all my customers: the starfish right at the bottom, on one breath. I say it's impossible, that even dolphins give up. Tourists love it. They all try, they all come up red as lobsters, and they rent a pedalo to recover. Thanks, Kevin.
textes.À tout le monde ! Voilà ! Une bonne nouv: Everyone! That's it! Good news is like a bubble: if you squeeze it in your hand, it bursts. If you let it go, it rises, and everyone sees it. Come on, there's room on my bench.
textes.À tout le monde… Hmm. Oui. Peut-être. Mê: To everyone… Hmm. Yes. Perhaps. Even the best. Even… No. Let's change the subject. Gaston, change the subject.
textes.À treize ans, j'ai tissé mon premier hui: At thirteen, I wove my first huipil all by myself, with the diamond of the world in the middle and its four corners. I had tied my loom to a young ceiba, behind the house. I pulled so hard that the tree leaned towards me. By the end, it was all bent. It still is. People call it “the tree that bows to Ix Sak”.
textes.À trente ans, j'ai creusé ma première ga: At thirty, I dug my very own first tunnel. Beautiful, straight, with a little nook for the lantern. The next day, I couldn't find it anywhere. Fifty years later, while enlarging my cellar, I fell right into it. It had been behind my house all along. The lantern was still there. Out, but offended.
At thirty, I took over Lisse & Son. I took over the office, the motto and my father's tie. “Demolish. Build. Cash in.” I demolished a lot. I built a lot. I cashed in enormously. The tie is a bit tight. It has always been a bit tight. I suppose that's the point of a tie.
textes.À trente ans, j'ai traversé la grande te: At thirty, I sailed through the great ash storm. The volcano was spitting, the sky was black at noon, and the waves were grey and as tall as… as the lighthouse. At least. I brought the Firebrand back to port with the whole crew, and a whale that followed us out of curiosity. I tell this story every evening. The waves grow a little bigger each time.
textes.À trente ans, j'ai volé la soucoupe de m: When I was thirty, I stole my aunt's saucer to fly around the Spire. Eighty-seven times. My aunt punished me: no flying for ten years. I spent ten years running in the Zero-Gravity Garden. Result: on top of everything, I run faster than everyone.

At thirty, I stole my aunt's saucer to fly around the Spire. Eighty-seven times. The whole island came out to watch. My aunt grounded me: no flying for ten years. I spent those ten years running in the Zero-Gravity Garden. Result: on top of everything, I run faster than anyone. Thanks, auntie.
textes.À trente ans, j'ai épousé Albert. Lui fa: At thirty, I married Albert. He made the jams, I did the accounts. He stirred his cauldrons whistling, I kept an eye on the sugar. We opened the delicatessen together. The first year, a lad “borrowed” an apple from me, promising to pay for it when he was mayor. He is mayor. He hasn't paid.
textes.À trois ans, j'ai pris une casserole et: At three, I grabbed a saucepan and a wooden spoon. At four, there wasn't a single saucepan left undented in Rainville. At five, Mother Downpour gave me a drum kit. To save the saucepans.
textes.À un ami ! Ce sont souvent les plus beau: To a friend! Those are often the loveliest bouquets. Nobody expects them, so they give twice the pleasure. For a friend, I recommend lavender. It lasts, like friendship.
textes.À un Égyptien ! Il l'a regardée, elle l': To an Egyptian! He looked at her, she looked at him, and they hit it off!
textes.À une réunion du jury, j'ai demandé, trè: At a jury meeting, I asked, very officially, for the automaton to be opened. “To see the dwarf.” Ambroise went white, then bright red, and said: “There isn't room.” That's not an answer. That's a measurement.
textes.À vingt ans, c'est moi qui conduisais. O: At twenty, I was the one driving. We called that locomotive “the Bielle” — the Crank: she creaked all over, but she never missed a climb. Fifteen years on the line. In the cab I always had a coffee pot on the boiler, and I served coffee to the shepherds at every stop. They said it was the best coffee in the highlands. It was the only one.
textes.À vingt ans, en creusant pour aider ma m: At twenty, digging to help my mother, I found a hot spring that smelled of eggs and bubbled. I sat down in it. I didn't come out for three hours. The next day, I built a pool. Then a second. Then a counter. That was the Sulphur Baths. I still haven't come out.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai décidé de faire toutes: At twenty, I decided to go to every party in the archipelago. The lighthouse ball in Port-Azur, the bonfires on the beaches, weddings, christenings, boat launches. They called me “the dancer who shows up before the music”. I wore out forty pairs of shoes. I kept them all. Well, thirty-eight. The dwarves kept two.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai embarqué comme cartogr: At twenty, I signed on as cartographer aboard an exploration ship. Forty islands, three seas, coasts no one had ever drawn. And a continent. Magnificent. With rivers, mountains, a heart-shaped bay. It didn't exist: it was a very well-formed bank of fog. But the map, my friend, the map was splendid.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai formé ma première lant: At twenty, I shaped my first lantern. Heavy as a cooking pot, and ugly as a cooking pot. A skinny kid, apprenticed to the old lantern-maker, took it without asking and pierced it all night long. In the morning, it cast stars on the wall. That was Nourredine. Forty years we've been arguing, ever since. The lantern, I don't know what became of it. Melted down, surely.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai obtenu de la vieille A: At twenty, I got a stony plot from the old Archduchess, south of the Lower Town, near the hot springs. Everyone laughed: nothing grows on stone. I carried the ash bucket by bucket, and watered with hot water. Three hundred years later, it's the Ash Gardens. Nobody laughs any more. Except me, with happiness.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai pris le Funiculaire av: At twenty, I took the Funicular with a single suitcase, full of empty notebooks. I went straight to the Observation Bay. A young oceanographer, who wasn't yet president, told me: “Sit down and say nothing.” After an hour, the Great Singer went by. I said nothing. I wept. Today, all the notebooks are full. I had to buy another suitcase.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai repris la petite parap: At twenty, I took over Mama's little umbrella shop, on the ground floor of number 7. I sew the canopies of the propeller umbrellas that Madame Bricolette sells at the Bazaar: double stitching, otherwise the propeller tears them at the first gust of wind. Achille wrecked one a week for me, “for tests”. I made him pay in washing-up. He did the dishes for ten years.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai voulu voir où allait l: At twenty, I wanted to see where the ice went when it left. I climbed onto a big ice floe, in spring, and let it drift south. Forty days. It melted the very evening it touched the beach of Arcanelle. I took that as a sign. That was sixty years ago. I haven't had another ice floe since.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai voulu être aventurière: At twenty, I wanted to be an adventurer. I had a ladle, a cauldron and plenty of courage. I knocked out a goblin, then found him so skinny I made him soup. He left with the recipe. The Guild told me that wasn't the idea. So I set up in its kitchen.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai été l'assistant d'un v: At twenty, I was assistant to an old lighthouse keeper. He had an emergency radio, and every evening he read the weather to the boats. One evening, he had a sore throat. He passed me the mic. I read the weather. A fisherman answered: “Thanks, lad.” I knew then that this was my job.
textes.À vingt ans, j'ai été maître-nageuse sur: At twenty, I was a lifeguard on a beach in Port-Azur. There was just one detail: I couldn't swim. I watched very, very carefully. I never left my chair. Nobody drowned all summer. I think it was the look in my eye. They called me Sirène to mock me. I kept the nickname out of pride.
textes.À vingt ans, j'étais fiancée à Jules, un: At twenty, I was engaged to Jules, a sailor from Port-Azur who whistled off-key and laughed just right. He signed on to a three-master, the Fair Star, to earn enough for us to settle down. On the quay, I promised him I'd hear the bell ring for his return. That same year, my father entrusted me with the key to the clock. I took it the way you take a promise: with both hands.
textes.À vingt ans, j'étais le meilleur danseur: At twenty, I was the best dancer in Tortuga. Yes, really. One evening, I went to sing under a lady's window, Mathilde, to invite her to the harbour ball. She answered with a pot of geraniums. On my head. The next day, I signed on to the first brig that came along. Years later, I named my ship the Veuve Écarlate. Scarlet, like her geraniums.
textes.À vingt ans, je me suis assis sur la Gra: At twenty, I sat down on the Great Square and began a story. Three people stopped. The next day, thirty. The day after that, the old Archduchess came to listen, disguised as a turnip seller. I recognised her by her horns. I said nothing. In six hundred years, I've never betrayed a hood.
textes.À vingt ans, je suis devenu cartographe: At twenty, I became the king's cartographer. He wanted the most accurate map in the world: I put in every tree, every pond, every cow. Eleven years of work. They stored it folded up in a barn, and the king asked me for a pocket version. During those eleven years, Mireille married the lighthouse keeper. At least he came home in the evenings. I shall say no more.
textes.À vingt ans, je suis devenu docker sur l: At twenty, I became a docker on the Old Dock. Barricade, who was forty-eight, carried two crates. I carried four. I was proud. She said to me: “It's not strength that counts, lad. It's gentleness in strength.” I didn't know what that meant. It took me ten years to understand.
textes.À vingt ans, je suis entrée à la Bibliot: At twenty, I joined the Library of Souls as an assistant librarian. Here, every demon in Pandémonia deposits the book of their life, which they write themselves. Some are three pages long, others three thousand. Grandpa Ébène's book takes up a whole shelf. Half of it is made up. He readily admits it.
textes.À vingt ans, je suis monté aux Nuées pou: At twenty, I came up to the Clouds for one summer, as a waiter. Water boiled so fast that my tea was ready before I was. I thought: now there's a place for a man in a hurry. I stayed forty years. I'm still not in a hurry. But my tea is.
textes.À vingt ans, je suis parti porter des va: At twenty, I went off to carry suitcases at the Grand Hotel in Port-Azur. One day, they redid the ballroom and dumped four old speakers on the quay. I brought them back on Barnabé's boat, with him at the helm. Seventeen crossings for the whole wall, plus forty of Octave's brackets, paid in cash. Gaston shouted “Shipwreck!” at every departure. We never sank.
textes.À vingt ans, je suis partie à Forgefer,: At twenty, I went to Forgefer, under Fire Mountain. One winter in the forge of Borin Ironbeard. I swept. I watched. They found me too hairy. I found them too chatty. Borin refused to teach me the runes. I came back with tempering. And this: a star-shaped burn, on my paw. Hm. A souvenir.
textes.À vingt ans, l'ancien intendant est part: When I was twenty, the old steward retired. He handed me a ring of a hundred keys and a six-hundred-page notebook. On the last page he had written: “Good luck. He loses everything.” I read the notebook in one night. The next day, the Baron had lost the key ring. I'd already had a copy made.
textes.À vingt ans, le vieux crieur public de P: When I was twenty, Pandémonia's old town crier lost his voice. He was looking for someone to replace him. I shouted “ME!” from the market, and he heard me from the palace. I got the job that very day. Since then, I've shouted the news every morning. Asmodin says I do it under his windows on purpose. It's true.
textes.À vingt ans, mon maître m'a emmené faire: At twenty, my master took me round the island. In Carène, it was the hungry winter: Yann-le-Borgne sold us the logbook of the Léviathan for semolina and dates, while his grandson, Corentin, listened under the table. Then we climbed up to Ramure, in the mists, and I spent a full-moon night swapping tales with a young bear. Tilleul.
textes.À vingt ans, mon père est tombé malade,: When I was twenty, my father fell ill, and the boat in the yard was half built. I finished it alone. On launch day, she floated crooked. A whole morning, in front of the whole quay. At noon, the wood drank up the water, and she straightened. My father came, leaning on my mother. He looked at her for a long time. He said: “Repaint her.”
textes.À vingt ans, à la Foire, il y avait une: When I was twenty, at the Fair, there was a glassblower at the next stand. She blew glass, I blew soap. Her name was Lise. She gave me a glass bubble “that never bursts”. It's on my bedside table. We married the following spring, and then Margot came along, with her mother's seriousness and my taste for round things.
textes.À vingt-cinq ans, j'ai fait ma première: At twenty-five, I made my first official forecast at the Institute: “Shower at twelve minutes past three.” At twelve minutes past three, it rained. On Hautefond. Two hundred metres below us. Right on time. The Council hesitated between sacking me and decorating me. It decorated me. For precision.
textes.À vingt-cinq ans, j'ai ouvert le Bazar d: At twenty-five, I opened the Bazaar in Papa's old shed. The house rule was born on the very first day: I buy back failed inventions, because they tried, by golly! The first item in the window was a compass that points south. Always south, faithful as a dog. I've sold it eleven times. It always comes back.
textes.À vingt-cinq ans, j'ai posé une grille s: At twenty-five, I set a grill on three stones at the end of the quay, next to the fish auction. Six sardines, a piece of bread, a pinch of Lalla Aïcha's cumin. The first day I sold four plates. The second, ten. That was twenty years ago. The three stones are still there. I've just changed the grill. Seven times.
textes.À vingt-cinq ans, j'ai répondu à une pet: At twenty-five, I answered a small advertisement: “Grand Hotel seeks serious receptionist.” I was serious. Forty-two windows, every one facing the sea, ordered by a shipowner who got seasick. He left after one night, green as a curtain. I've been here thirty years. Still serious, I dare to hope.
textes.À vingt-cinq ans, je suis allé à la fête: At twenty-five, I went to the Dawn festival with a basket of turnips. One of them escaped, crossed the dance floor and leapt into a young woman's arms. She caught it one-handed, without even looking, and kept on dancing. That was Germaine. I said to myself: she's the one. So did the turnip, I think.
textes.À vingt-deux ans, j'ai fondé la Gazette: At twenty-two, I founded the Cogs Gazette with my father's old steam press. A marvel. It misses one letter in a hundred, it spits ink on Tuesdays and it whistles at commas. At first I was ashamed of the typos. Then readers started hunting for them, pencil in hand. Now, if there aren't any, they complain!
textes.À vingt-deux ans, j'ai pris les clés de: At twenty-two, I took the keys to the observatory. It had been empty since the old astronomer died: cobwebs right into the eyepiece. I spent a year cleaning the great telescope, screw by screw. The first night it was clean, I saw the rings of a planet. I cried. Since then, I've lived at night. By day, I sleep. Coffee bridges the gap.
textes.À vingt-deux ans, le vieux gardien m'a p: At twenty-two, the old keeper took me on as his assistant. I didn't like the sea up close. It's wet, it shouts. From up high, it's quiet. That was forty years ago. I go up at sunset, come down at dawn, three hundred and twenty steps each time. And every night, one page of the logbook. The wind, the boats, the lights. Hardly anything else.
At ten p.m., I go into standby. I dream in power-saving mode. I dream about the tour. It goes very well.
textes.À vingt-quatre ans, j'ai fait construire: At twenty-four, I had Ali build my boat. Twenty days in the boatyard. Three coats of blue, because two wasn't blue enough. Ali painted the eye on the prow; it's a little cross-eyed. I named her the Zahra, after my grandmother. She judged everything by eye, so her boat needed an eye.
textes.À vingt-sept ans, j'ai pris un sac, douz: At twenty-seven, I took a bag, twelve new notebooks and my worst shoes: I was saving the good ones for the way back. Mistake. The highlands, where the shepherds gave me cheese and not a word; the desert, where the dunes move at night; the mists. Two months. I came back barefoot, with the first real map of the island.
textes.À voix basse, et faux. Elles ont entendu: Under your breath, and out of tune. They heard.
textes.ÇA MORD, HURLA ! ET TOI, ÇA CRIE ?: THEY'RE BITING, HURLA! AND YOU, ARE YOU SHOUTING?
textes.Ça ? C'est un champignon des fées. Il po: That? It's a fairy mushroom. It grows in the circle behind the dune, on nights when the music is beautiful. If you nibble it, you take a trip… to the fairy kingdom, above the clouds, where the Yggdrasil tree grows. Here, take it. Up there, you'll arrive in a circle of mushrooms: when you want to come back, step inside it, and it will bring you back here, on the beach. (In your bag: “Use”.)
textes.Ça a marché !!! Maître ! Vous êtes redev: It worked!!! Master! You're yourself again! Thank you, thank you! Here, take this, it's a successful potion. I think.
textes.Ça arrive aux voyageurs. On part si loin: That happens to travellers. You go so far you no longer know who's watching the door. Write to them. And meanwhile, eat.
textes.Ça avait encore le goût des vacances, ma: Did my soup still taste of holidays?
textes.Ça avance, ça avance !: It's coming along, it's coming along!
textes.Ça chatouille ?! Je veux essayer ! Non,: It tickles?! I want to try! No, Mama says no. But where does it tickle? Your feet? Your ears? Both?
textes.Ça compte, derrière un nuage ?: Does it count, behind a cloud?
textes.Ça dépend ! Tu parles comme Gaubert. Lui: It depends! You sound like Gaubert. He keeps secrets “depending”, too. And I know he's keeping one. I can feel it. He smiles too much.
textes.Ça dépend ! Ça, c'est une réponse de vra: Depends! Now that's a real merchant's answer. You know what? You and me, we'll open a shop one day. You do the smiles, I'll do the till.
textes.Ça dépend ? Ah, une âme de marchande ! U: It depends? Ah, a merchant's soul! A little secret, you keep; a big one, you sell dear. I respect that.
textes.Ça dépend ? Comme la Grande Perle, alors: It depends? Like the Great Pearl, then! White in the morning, purple in the evening! But the real one does it all by itself, without anybody pressing a button? … The sky must be really clever.
textes.Ça dépend ? Intéressant. Très intéressan: It depends? Interesting. Very interesting. You're the caravan-trader kind, you are: nobody ever knows what you're thinking. I'm going to keep an eye on you, my friend.
textes.Ça dépend de l'eau, tu as dit. … Tu avai: Depends on the water, you said. … You were right. Still water. Beware.
It depends on the time and the weather.
textes.Ça dépend de nous… Tu parles comme un pr: It depends on us… You speak like a priest of Aztlán. There's hope for you. Come to the calmecac one day.
textes.Ça dépend de qui écoute, disiez-vous… J': It depends on who's listening, you said… I think of it at every speech.
textes.Ça dépend de quoi. Hm. C'est la réponse: “It depends on what.” Hm. That's an old man's answer. Or a wise man's. You're too young to be old.
textes.Ça dépend du chat, m'avais-tu dit. Le ro: Depends on the cat, you told me. The ginger one doesn't depend on anything. He's a demon.
textes.Ça dépend du jour ! Sage réponse. Le mat: It depends on the day! A wise answer. Quiet in the morning; the Arena in the afternoon! That's exactly my day. Well, without the quiet morning.
textes.Ça dépend lesquels… Voilà une réponse di: Depends which ones… Now there's an answer worthy of an amin. The cabin boy, yes. The cook, for his cooking, no. The captain… we'll see. You've got an eye, you have.
textes.Ça dépend. Tu es venu pour m'embêter ?: Depends. Have you come to bother me?
textes.Ça dépend. Voilà une réponse de marin. O: It depends. That's a sailor's answer. You keep what floats and let the rest sink. Except boots. Boots, you keep: you never know when the other one will fall.
textes.Ça dépend… Oui. Une bêtise, oui. Un mens: It depends… Yes. Something silly, yes. A lie, maybe. A lost ring, apparently yes. I'll let you know if it works.
textes.Ça dépend… Tu as raison. On attend une b: It depends… You're right. We'll wait all night for a boat without noticing the time, and get worked up waiting five minutes for a sardine. Patience is knowing what's worth it.
textes.Ça fait cinq ans que je fais les chambre: I've been doing the rooms at the Grand Hôtel for five years. On my first day, Monsieur Edmond taught me hospital corners: the sheet folded neatly on the diagonal, tucked in so tight a coin would bounce off it. And I soon understood the rest: a bed tells you everything. Who sleeps badly, who sleeps alone, who eats biscuits in secret.
textes.Ça fait huit cents ans que je fais la si: I've been napping for eight hundred years. It's a very, very big nap.
textes.Ça fait trois fois que je reviens. Le fo: This is the third time I've come back. The pink form was blue.
textes.Ça fait {absence}. Je croyais que les cr: It's been {absence}. I thought the crabs had got you. Or worse: Barnabé.
That sounds nicely gritty, right there.
textes.Ça irait mieux avec du bois. Il n'y a pa: It would be better with some wood. There are no trees in the desert. I have to buy it in Carène, and they sell it dear.
textes.Ça irait mieux avec un cochonnet. On jou: It'd be better with a jack. We're playing with a pebble, it's a disgrace.
textes.Ça irait mieux si Gontran Jambe-de-Bois: I'd be better if Gontran Jambe-de-Bois paid his debts. Forty coins! Three moons I've been waiting!
textes.Ça irait mieux si j'avais mes dorades. L: It would be better if I had my sea bream. Friday's tajine can't be made with sardines!
textes.Ça irait mieux si l'étal d'à côté vendai: It'd be better if the stall next door sold flowers. Atchoo.
textes.Ça joue fort ! Très fort ! Le lustre se: It's loud! Very loud! The chandelier swings in rhythm.
textes.Ça marche aussi ! Les plantes aiment tou: That works too! Plants love all kinds of music. Even slightly off-key whistling.
That reminds me of a star.
textes.Ça me va ! Mais tu reviens, hein ?: That'll do! But you'll come back, eh?
textes.Ça monte ! Prochain arrêt : le Belvédère: Going up! Next stop: the Belvedere, sixty metres up.
textes.Ça monte, ça descend… Moi, je reste assi: Up it goes, down it goes… Me, I stay sitting down. That's how I travel.
textes.Ça monte, ça monte… !: Here it comes, here it comes…!
textes.Ça mord pas, aujourd'hui. Même les poiss: Nothing's biting today. Even the fish are on strike.
They bite if you're quiet, Tibo.
They bite if you keep quiet.
textes.Ça mord, en ce moment ?: Are they biting at the moment?
textes.Ça mord, par ici ?: Are the fish biting around here?
textes.Ça n'existe pas, Pétronille. … Mais oui,: There's no such thing, Pétronille. … But yes, please.
It wasn't supposed to do that.
textes.Ça ne me dit rien. Elle est bonne, ta bi: Doesn't ring a bell. Is it any good, your fizz?
textes.Ça ne me dit rien. … Ta blonde est trop: Doesn't ring a bell. … Your golden fizz is too golden.
textes.Ça ne rime pas du tout, Lyre !: That doesn't rhyme at all, Lyre!
textes.Ça ne sent pas la soupe, aujourd'hui: It doesn't smell of soup today
textes.Ça ne sent pas la soupe, aujourd'hui…: It doesn't smell of soup today…
textes.Ça ne sert à rien ? Essaie avec une foug: Pointless? Try it with a fern. Ferns adore compliments.
textes.Ça plane ! Prochain arrêt : la Gare des: All's breezy! Next stop: Cloud Station, a hundred and thirty metres up.
textes.Ça pèse ! C'est de la farine, ou des pav: It's heavy! Is this flour, or cobblestones?
textes.Ça redonne du courage ! +1 de force pend: That perks you up! +1 strength for two minutes.
textes.Ça remue dans les bosquets… un groin ros: Something is rustling in the bushes… a pink and black snout appears, sniffs, and vanishes. Truffe is there, but he's shy. With his little bell, he'd recognise you!
textes.Ça rit tellement fort ici que la vaissel: The laughter is so loud here that the dishes rattle on the shelves.
textes.Ça ronfle. Fort. Sur une natte, un petit: Snoring. Loudly. On a mat, a little Moai sleeps, covered in moss.
textes.Ça réchauffe ! +1 de force pendant deux: It warms you up! +1 strength for two minutes.
textes.Ça sent bon par ici. Ça sent bon partout: It smells good around here. It smells good everywhere, actually.
textes.Ça sent l'huile et le brûlé. Au fond, un: It smells of oil and burning. At the back, a machine full of indicator lights blinks cheerfully.
textes.Ça sent l'huile fine et le laiton. Parto: It smells of fine oil and brass. Everywhere, pendulums swing to and fro, like a forest breathing.
textes.Ça sent l'huile fine et le papier à dess: It smells of fine oil and drawing paper. A little drone flies in circles under the ceiling; a mechanical arm waves at you from the workbench.
It smells of beard oil and rivalry. In front of the mirror, two dwarves compare their braids.
textes.Ça sent la chouquette chaude et le lait: It smells of warm sugar puffs and frothy milk. At the Cumulus Café, everyone has a white moustache, and nobody dares tell anyone else.
textes.Ça sent la fumée et le vieux bois. « App: It smells of smoke and old wood. “Come closer, traveler,” says a stone voice, slow and gentle.
textes.Ça sent la menthe et le miel. Autour d'u: It smells of mint and honey. Around a low table, a family sips herbal teas from mismatched cups.
textes.Ça sent la menthe fraîche. Autour d'une: It smells of fresh mint. Around a small low table, cushions of every color.
textes.Ça sent la mousse et le champignon. C'es: It smells of moss and mushrooms. It's nice. I'm making a note.
textes.Ça sent la peinture fraîche. Des bâches: It smells of fresh paint. Tarps everywhere, a ladder, paint pots… A house in the middle of a makeover.
textes.Ça sent la peinture à l'huile. Des toile: It smells of oil paint. Canvases everywhere, and an artist squinting at you: “You! You have an interesting face!”
textes.Ça sent la pomme, la terre et le bois mo: It smells of apples, earth and damp wood. Today's harvest is being sorted.
textes.Ça sent la soupe. Une soupe épaisse, mys: It smells of soup. A thick, mysterious soup… and oddly mineral.
It smells of wet earth and strawberries. A little drone buzzes past: “Pschhh!” A fern says thank you.
textes.Ça sent le blé chaud. La grande roue de: It smells of warm wheat. The great wooden wheel creaks above your head, like an old ship.
textes.Ça sent le café des sommets et le papier: It smells of summit coffee and map paper. On the wall, a board lists the departures; on the ceiling, a little glider goes round in circles.
It smells of hot chocolate and vanilla. Someone pours a brown, foamy liquid from one pot to another, from very, very high.
textes.Ça sent le chocolat et le pain grillé. A: It smells of chocolate and toast. In the middle of the table, a copper machine whistles, puffs… and launches slices of toast.
It smells of leather and knight's oil. A suit of armor shines against the wall.
textes.Ça sent le cuir et la toile cirée. Des c: It smells of leather and oilcloth. Wind maps, a compass, and a miniature airship doing its rounds above everyone's heads.
textes.Ça sent le feu de bois, la noix de coco: It smells of wood smoke, coconut and grilled fish. At the back, a pile of stones smokes gently.
textes.Ça sent le gâteau chaud. Dans la cuisine: It smells like warm cake. In the kitchen, someone is taking a tray out of the oven.
textes.Ça sent le printemps et le volcan ! (Il: It smells of spring and volcano! (He kneads, he bakes, and the Eternal Oven purrs.) And there you go: three honey cakes, piping hot. One per head, mind! Don't eat them on the way.
textes.Ça sent le sel, l'encre et le café froid: It smells of salt, ink and cold coffee. The clerk stamps, the sailors wait.
It smells of flowers and damp earth. In one corner, a glass greenhouse and its little fountain; everywhere else, butterflies.
textes.Ça suffit ! Lève les poings, si t'en as: That's enough! Put your fists up, if you've got the guts!
textes.Ça tourne, ça tourne… on se croirait dan: Round and round it goes… it's like being inside a clockmaker's head.
textes.Ça va ! Rien n'a explosé aujourd'hui. En: Fine! Nothing exploded today. Well, almost nothing.
textes.Ça va ?! Comment ça, ça va ? … T'es mala: Fine?! What d'you mean, fine? … You sick? Go see Doc. Somebody who's not hungry, that ain't normal.
textes.Ça va cogner ! Prévenez le Doc, il va av: Fists are flying! Warn the Doc, he's got work coming!
textes.Ça va faire plaisir aux salades d'en hau: That'll please the lettuces up top.
That's better! Let's get back to it… gently.
textes.Ça va mieux depuis que tu passes. Ne t'h: Better since you started dropping by. Don't get used to it, I'm still an old bear.
textes.Ça va mieux, ta faim ? La dernière fois,: Is your hunger better? Last time, you weren't hungry. I couldn't sleep over it.
textes.Ça va mieux, ton mal du pays ? Je t'ai g: Feeling less homesick? I've kept you the seat by the cauldron. It's the warmest on the island.
It'll come back, it'll come back.
textes.Ça va. Douze bateaux sont entrés, douze: Fine. Twelve boats came in, twelve went out. Nobody fell in the water. Well, yes: a crate of Rosalie's apples. The gulls were very pleased.
textes.Ça va. La lumière du jour me fait cligne: I'm all right. Daylight makes me blink. I'm a night demon. With little wings. They don't fly. They're decorative.
textes.Ça va. Le soufflet tire bien, le fer cha: Fine. The bellows are blowing well, the iron's heating, nobody's bothering me. Well, almost nobody.
textes.Ça va… Merci de demander. Personne ne de: I'm all right… Thanks for asking. Nobody ever asks the bassist.
That means thank you, I know.
textes.Ça vibre, ça chante tout bas. Un technic: It vibrates, it sings under its breath. A technician smiles: “It likes you. It does that with people it likes.”
It comes from very far away.
textes.Ça y est, j'ai soufflé ! Me revoilà, ave: There, I've caught my breath! I'm back, with my prayers!
textes.Ça, alors ! Ton cadeau brille plus qu'un: Well, I never! Your gift shines brighter than a lanternfish! Thank you, {surnom}. All of Pearl Square is going to hear about it.
textes.Ça, c'est Icare Plané et son école. Ils: That's Icare Plané and his school. They take off from the end of the pier and glide around the island. Word is, Icare hasn't walked anywhere in three years.
Now that's some fine scrap metal.
Now that's wood. Nice and dry, nice and straight.
textes.Ça, c'est du solide, comme réponse. Une: Now that's a solid answer. A blade that never breaks never needs replacing. Bad for business. Excellent for you.
textes.Ça, c'est du vent !: Now that's what I call wind!
That one's going in my Big Notebook.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau ! Je ne l'oublierai: Now that's a present! I won't forget it, {surnom}.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau de Frondeur ! Merci,: Now that's a Frondeur's gift! Thanks, {surnom}. I'll tell the whole Assembly about it. Twice. And we'll vote on whether it's the best gift of the week.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau de héros ! Merci, {s: Now that's a hero's gift! Thank you, {surnom}. I'll tell the whole Great Square about it.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau de punk au grand cœu: Now that's a big-hearted punk's gift! Thanks, {surnom}. I'm going to tell the whole of Pallet Square.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau qui brille plus qu'u: Now that's a gift that shines brighter than a crystal from the mine! Thank you, {surnom}. All of Cogwheel Square is going to hear about it.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau qui fait du bien ! M: Now that's a gift that does you good! Thank you, {surnom}. I can feel my flame growing.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau qui plane ! Merci, {: Now that's a gift that flies high! Thank you, {surnom}. The whole Esplanade will hear about it.
textes.Ça, c'est un cadeau tout en haut de l'éc: Now that's a top-floor gift! Thank you, {surnom}. The whole Square is going to hear about it.
textes.Ça, c'est un vrai cadeau ! Merci, {surno: Now that's a real gift! Thank you, {surnom}. My heart is as light as Maât's feather.
Now that was a lovely crossing.
That, you'll have to ask her.
textes.Ça, je ne sais pas le soigner. Toi non p: That, I don't know how to cure. Nor do you.
That, I'll tell you another time. When we're better friends.
textes.Ça, je vous le raconterai une autre fois: That, I'll tell you another time. When we know each other better.
textes.Ça, une barbe ? Un paillasson, oui !: That, a beard? A doormat, more like!
textes.Éblouie. Le blanc des maisons, le bleu d: Dazzled. The white of the houses, the blue of the doors, the ochre of the ramparts… I don't have enough colours.
textes.Ébène dit qu'au fond des Neuf Cercles, à: Ébène says that at the bottom of the Nine Circles, in Malebolge, the bridges turn. Advice from an old guard: don't run on a moving bridge. Wait until it stops in front of you. A turning bridge is like a hesitant customer: it always makes up its mind in the end.
textes.Ébène dit qu'il y a une Tourmente dans l: Ébène says there's a Tempest in the Nine Circles, with terrible gusts. Postwoman's tip: never push against a gust; wait for it to pass and dart through between two. And the gargoyles in the ruins? I avoid them. They love postbags.
textes.Ébène dit que Cerbère adore les gâteaux: Ébène says Cerbère loves honey cakes
Ébène says Cerbère loves honey cakes…
textes.Ébène et moi, nous nous connaissons depu: Ébène and I have known each other for three centuries. He tells stories, I listen. He cheats at draughts, I pretend not to see. That's what an old friendship is.
textes.Ébène raconte aux enfants que les Neuf C: Ébène tells the children the Nine Circles were dug by a giant with a spoon, to store the cold in. Then I explain that the founders dug them over a thousand years, with pickaxes and plans. The children prefer the spoon. I asked them why. They answered: “Because it's better.” I didn't know what to say.
textes.Ébène, je suis directeur. Et j'ai trois: Ébène, I'm the headmaster. And I'm three hundred years old.
textes.Ébène, la bataille des Cendres, c'était: Ébène, the battle of the Ashes was five hundred years ago. Not a thousand.
textes.Écho m'a dit bonjour, ce matin. Un mot e: Écho said hello to me this morning. A whole word! I told the entire Canteen.
textes.Écho m'a dit quatre mots, ce matin. Quat: Écho said four words to me this morning. Four! “Your guitar's out of tune.” He was right. The low E. He can hear it from the other end of the cavern. With ears like his, he could tune the Column.
textes.Écho parle quatre mots par jour, et ils: Écho speaks four words a day, and they're always the right ones. He can hear an out-of-tune string from the other end of the cavern. He rocked Ysaé to sleep with his bass. He's the quiet big brother of the whole Fronde.
textes.Écho, ce n'est pas mon vrai nom. C'est B: Écho isn't my real name. Brasero gave it to me, the day I arrived. I'd only said one word all evening. He said: “That one repeats what the rock says.” My real first name… (He shrugs.) I lent it to the Chasm. It's keeping it safe.
Écho, I've written a song about you.
textes.Écho. Ça va, à la Fronde ?: Écho. How are things in the Fronde?
textes.Éclair ! (Un grand craquement.) … Les cr: Lightning! (A great crack.) … The crystals are singing. They're happy.
textes.Éclair ! Et pas une étincelle sur mon ch: Lightning! And not one spark on my hat! A record!
textes.Éclair ! … Ah. Il est revenu. Sur moi. C: Bolt! … Ah. It came back. Onto me. As usual.
textes.Éclair ? Rapide. Très rapide. Silencieus: Éclair? Fast. Very fast. Silent. She never says anything, but she looks at me as if I were a finish line. That's racing. Hop.
textes.Éclair et moi, on partage la maison du G: Éclair and I share the house at the Lookout. We can spend a whole evening without a word. That's rare, someone you can be comfortable in silence with.
textes.Éclair ne dit jamais rien, mais elle me: Éclair never says a word, but she looks at me like I'm a kebab. I don't like it.
textes.Éclair ne dit jamais rien. Jamais ! Et e: Éclair never says anything. Ever! And she looks at me like I'm a skewer. Me, a skewer! I don't know what I did to her, but it must be serious.
Éclair trains in secret, at night. I've seen her. She didn't see me. I'm too fast.
textes.Éclairer toute la cité sans une goutte d: Light up the whole city without a drop of oil. One night, all at once, every street at the same time, right down to the lower alleys. And see Professor Boum's face at that moment. Especially that. I'll put my glasses on, to get a good look.
textes.Écliptique a décrété le troisième banc d: Écliptique decreed the third bench of the Agora protocolary. I went and sat on it at ten p.m. sharp, to tease him. He started drafting a decree to evict me. At five past ten, I went home to bed. He finished his decree at midnight. The bench had been free for ages.
textes.Écliptique a fait encadrer mon poème de: Écliptique had my four-word poem framed in the Council Chamber. He didn't understand it was a joke. Or maybe he did, and framed it anyway. With him, you never know.
textes.Écliptique a proposé une nouvelle règle: Écliptique proposed a new rule for electing the Elder: votes, hats, speeches. We voted. We kept my rule, the one where it's the oldest. He made a speech to congratulate the rule. It was very beautiful, and it lasted twelve minutes.
textes.Écliptique a préparé un discours de bien: Écliptique has prepared an eleven-minute welcome speech for the next visitor. Halo has prepared a four-minute one. They're arguing over which one goes first. The visitor, meanwhile, has left.
textes.Écliptique croit qu'un discours doit êtr: Écliptique thinks a speech has to be long to be good. Eleven minutes! Mine is dense: every “welcome” counts. But I must admit he does very fine bows, when he doesn't fall over.
textes.Écliptique fait des règlements pour savo: Écliptique makes rules so he knows what to do with his hands. He falls a lot, he talks too much, and he's terribly kind, though he hides it under nine thousand articles.
textes.Écliptique m'a demandé un dôme protocola: Écliptique asked me for a ceremonial dome, with a stage. He fell off the stage on opening day. The stage was round too. He rolled.
textes.Écliptique m'a demandé un poème pour un: Écliptique asked me for a poem for an official speech. I gave him: “Écliptique, terrific, protocol, rigmarole.” As a joke. He had it framed in gold letters in the Council Chamber. Every visitor who reads it bursts out laughing. Écliptique says it's “poetic emotion”. I don't dare say anything anymore.
Écliptique asked me for a poem for an official speech. I wrote him: “Écliptique, so majestic, protocol, rigmarole.” He had it framed. He didn't realise it was a joke. Don't tell him.
textes.Écliptique m'a lu l'article douze de son: Écliptique read me article twelve of his rulebook, on bows. I answered: “I bow to you, great chief, but my back is far too brief.” He thought about it for a long time, then he added it to the rulebook: article twelve-bis. It's the only article in verse. He's very proud of it.
textes.Écliptique m'a marché sur les pieds tren: Écliptique stepped on my feet thirty-two times at the millennium ball. He apologised for six minutes. Since then, I've been giving him lessons in secret. He's improving. Now he only steps on one foot.
Écliptique talks a lot, and for a long time. I keep the time. It's my way of helping him. Without me, his speeches would last until the Night of the Auroras. Sometimes with me, too.
textes.Écliptique prétend que son discours est: Écliptique claims his speech is longer than mine. It lasts eleven minutes. But mine is denser. Every word counts. Especially “welcome”. I say it forty times.
